title: PLEASE TAKE NOTICE OF PLANNING COMMISSION PUBLIC HEARING NOVEMBER 18, 2026 AT 6:30 PM
text: AUGUSTA CHARTER TOWNSHIP NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING PLANNING COMMISSION Notice is hereby given that the Augusta Charter Township Planning Commission will hold a Public Hearing on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 6:30 p.m. at the Lincoln Senior Center, 8970 Whittaker Road (west entrance of Brick Elementary), Ypsilanti, MI 48197. The purpose of this public hearing is to receive public input and to consider a proposed amendment to the Augusta Charter Township Zoning Ordinance. The proposed amendment would establish a six (6) month temporary moratorium on certain zoning approvals and applications related to High Resource Demand Facilities, including data centers, while the Township reviews and develops zoning regulations addressing these facilities and their potential impacts on infrastructure, utilities, surrounding land uses, and public health, safety, and welfare. If you have any written comments or concerns, they can be sent to the Augusta Charter Township Planning Commission, P.O. Box 100, Whittaker, MI 48190-0100 or by email to the Township Clerk – clerk@augustatownship.org and should be received prior to 4:00 PM on November 18, 2026. A copy of the proposed ordinance amendment is available for public inspection at the Augusta Charter Township offices during regular business hours located at 8021 Talladay Rd, Willis, MI 48191. Augusta Township Planning Commission PUBLISH: November 1, 2026

title: November 10, 2026
text: East China Charter Township Official Board Minutes November 10, 2025 EAST CHINA CHARTER TOWNSHIP OFFICIAL PROCEEDINGS NOVEMBER 10, 2025 CALL TO ORDER – Supervisor Westrick called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m., with Clerk Smith, Treasurer Horn, and Trustees Kline, Babel, Reichle & Biebuyck. Also present: Director of Public Services, Dwayne Loper and Koryn Garwood, Bookkeeper. Thirty-five in the audience. PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE APPROVE AGENDA – Clerk Smith, supported by Treasurer Horn, moved to approve the Agenda. Carried. PUBLIC HEARING FOR 2026 BUDGETS Trustee Reichle, supported by Treasurer Horn, moved to open the 2026 Budget Public Hearing at 7:02 p.m. Carried. The proposed millage rates for the 2026 General Fund, Parks Fund, Capital Projects Fund, Building Inspection Fund, Water Fund, DPW Fund, and Sewer Fund Budgets are to be adopted in compliance with the State of Michigan Public Act 621 of 1978, which amends P.A. 2 of 1968 entitled, The Uniform Budgeting and Accounting Act. The two proposed millage rates are as follows: 4.2367 rate generates property tax revenues of $2,936,175 at taxable value of $693,033,589. This rate includes road improvements that were not originally planned for in the previous Budget Hearing. 4.3810 rate generates property tax revenues of $3,036,180 at taxable value of $693,033,589. This rate includes road improvements and $100,000 from the General Fund to help subsidize the substantial water and sewer rate increase. PUBLIC COMMENT – Evelyn Toles from the Park Commission shared information and pricing for park playground equipment to replace the Kid-E-Scape. Members reviewed figures towards this project and asked if the locomotive project funds could be applied to this project. The estimated pricing for this project is near $500,000. Residents asked questions about the water and sewer rates and how this figures into the 2026 Budget. East China Charter Township Official Board Minutes November 10, 2025 Trustee Reichle, supported by Trustee Babel, moved to close the Public Hearing at 7:15 p.m. Carried. PUBLIC COMMENT FOR WATER & SEWER RATES Lori Eschenburg, 4495 Clarke Drive reviewed information regarding the impacts of such a substantial increase in the water and sewer rates and how this will affect already strained, residents’ household expenses. Water consumption has decreased. She asked the Board to consider all financial resources to reduce the impact on our residents. She asked about our Capital Improvement Plan and balance of funds. Supervisor Westrick explained that members of the Board have had multiple water and sewer rate workshops to review all possible funding sources to cover the large debt that was incurred over the past couple years of new water main and sewer main replacements. Many options were considered. He explained that the new rate structure proposal has $25,000 per year for the CIP for water and $75,000 sewer each year + $20,000 sewer equipment replacement. He said that this new infrastructure should have been a voted millage to cover the $9.5 million debt. He also stated that the Township is in good financial condition. A resident said that the hose at the outside spigot at the water plant has many people coming during the night to fill large tanks and trucks. This water is not being paid for, which impacts the costs. Residents asked for more information regarding this whole process. They want to know how we got here and the details; what options are being considered when determining these water and sewer rates. Residents asked why a debt re-payment plan was not put into place for the $9.5 million when this loan was being applied for. Residents asked that oversight be put into place so that this does not happen again; where the residents will be charged such significant increases. Residents asked if there were experts consulted during this process regarding the rate recommendation. Residents asked about selling water to other communities. We have existing emergency Agreements in place for water and piping that connects to St. Clair and Marine City. Residents asked about China Township. East China supplies water to China Township at a cost. China Township is a partner in the water plant and is a member of the Water & Sewer Authority. Trustee Reichle stated that over the last 10-year period, we have paid over $1-million for senior management wages and benefits. He stated that we need to look at all areas in the budget to cut expenses. He suggested that we re-allocate the Capital Improvement Funds set aside for the new DPW building, and the funds for the Township Hall addition. That would add up to about $1million dollars. He said we have more staff in water and sewer than Marine City/St. Clair. Years ago, we had one Superintendent for both Water & Sewer Plants. We were the only one in the East China Charter Township Official Board Minutes November 10, 2025 County to have a Township Manager and Director of Public Services. He said the elected officials are not doing their job. He suggested reducing the wages of the Treasurer, Clerk, & Supervisor until they show what they are doing to fulfill their positions. He said we need to safeguard taxpayer money for the future and demand accountability. He said we are the highest water/sewer rates and taxes in the County. He said we have executive level staff doing elected Officials duties. He said we need to go line by line of each employee and cut what we don’t need. He said the Township Manager position was a failure. He said we have no summer recreation program. He said do away with the pension program for elected Officials. He said to look at different ways of managing staffing levels. Trustee Kline said that he has viewed the Capital Improvement Plan. We need to have funds set aside for the future in case something goes wrong. He agrees to look at all positions and review what is not needed. Then a $500,000 playground is introduced. We need to look at the Budget and see what is not needed. He suggested we subsidize the water and sewer rates this year with $1,000,000 Capital Improvement Funds that were set aside from DPW and Township Hall Buildings. He said next year we will need a new plan. Treasurer Horn said we need to review the next budget line by line at a budget meeting. She recommended not replacing the Director position. She recommended subsidizing the water/sewer rates with existing funds/Fund Balance. Clerk Smith said that all Departments are not overstaffed. The Manager position was created right before the major infrastructure project began, so that person could coordinate the project with the Engineers and Contractors. Trustee Babel asked who would absorb the workload of the Director if not replaced. Trustee Biebuyck said that a lot of work went into reviewing these water/sewer rates by attending workshops. We have a good township. She asked who would do these jobs of Clerk, Treasurer, Supervisor with zero pay. She is not in favor of ripping off the band-aid. She is a retiree also who will have a double digit increase in water/sewer charges. She does not like personal attacks on the Board. She has been the Deputy Clerk now for a year with a lot to learn. She will not argue on this Board between members. She asked to move NB-4 to after NB-1. Trustee Reichle, supported by Trustee Biebuyck, moved to change NB-1 to after NB-4. Carried. Trustee Reichle, supported by Trustee Kline, moved to change NB-2 to after NB-1. Carried. Members proposed that we use General Fund Balance to subsidize the water and sewer rates, adopting the 4.3810 millage rate, and taking the DPW Building and Township Hall addition funds reserve and using these funds to reduce the ready to serve charge. East China Charter Township Official Board Minutes November 10, 2025 NEW BUSINESS NB 3 - CLOSED SESSION FOR UNION CONTRACT NEGOTIATIONS Treasurer Horn, supported by Trustee Babel, moved to close the regular meeting and enter into Closed Session at 9:00 p.m. Carried. Trustee Reichle, supported by Trustee Kline, moved to open the regular meeting at 8:38 p.m. Carried. NB 4 – Director of Public Service Transition Plan Supervisor Westrick proposed that we not replace the Director position, and promote Bookkeeper Garwood to Township Office Supervisor. She would then move from the Clerical IUOE 324 unit to the Supervisor IUOE Unit. This would maintain continuity within our organizational structure. All four Department Supervisor’s would report to the Township Supervisor. He is looking into contracting with our Township Planner from Wade-Trim for one day per week inhouse for grant writing purposes and project planning. Clerk Smith, supported by Treasurer Horn, moved to postpone action of promoting the Bookkeeper to Office Supervisor, until the next meeting November 17, 2025. Carried. NB 1 – Resolution 14-2025 Adopt the 2026 Budgets at 4.3810 Millage Rate RESOLUTION 14-2025 ADOPT 2026 BUDGETS FOR THE GENERAL FUND, PARKS FUND, CAPITAL PROJECTS FUND, BUILDING INSPECTION, WATER, SEWER & DPW FUNDS East China Charter Township County of St. Clair, Michigan Minutes of a regular meeting of the Township Board of Trustees of East China Township, County of St. Clair, Michigan, held in the Township Hall, on the 10TH day of November 2025 at 7:00 p.m. PRESENT: Westrick, Smith, Horn, Babel, Biebuyck, Reichle, Kline. ABSENT: None. The following Resolution was offered by Westrick and supported by Smith. WHEREAS, under the provisions of the Uniform Budgeting and Accounting Act 621 of 1978 for local units of government in Michigan, all budgets for the General Fund, Capital Projects Fund, and Debt Service Funds must be adopted by the Legislative Body, which is the East China Charter Township Board of Trustees, and East China Charter Township Official Board Minutes November 10, 2025 WHEREAS, the East China Charter Township Supervisor has submitted proposed 2026 Budgets for the General Fund, Parks Fund, Capital Projects Fund, Building Inspection Fund, Water Fund, DPW Fund and Sewer Fund using a cost center approach in accordance with the Uniform Budgeting and Accounting Act, P.A. 621 of 1978, and WHEREAS, pursuant to MCL 42.26, notice of a public hearing on the proposed budget was published in the Times Herald newspaper of general circulation on November 3, 2025, and a Public Hearing on the proposed budgets was held in the East China Charter Township Hall at 7:00 p.m. on November 10, 2025, and WHEREAS, estimated township general fund revenues for fiscal year 2026, including an allocated millage of: 4.3810 generates property tax revenues of $3,036,180 at taxable value of $ 693,033,589 WHEREAS, the East China Charter Township Board of Trustees is authorized to levy and collect general property taxes on all real and personal, property within the township upon the current tax rolls up to 5.0 mills for General Operations and up to the amounts necessary to service bonds voted by the electorate, NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the above recommended 2026 General Fund, Parks Fund, Capital Projects Fund, Building Inspection Fund, Water Fund, DPW Fund, and Sewer Fund Budgets be adopted in compliance with the State of Michigan Public Act 621 of 1978, which amends P. A. 2 of 1968 entitled, "The Uniform Budgeting and Accounting Act," and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the East China Charter Township levies the following millage for the 2026 fiscal year: East China Township Operating 4.3810 All resolutions and parts of resolutions insofar as they conflict with the provisions of this Resolution be and the same hereby are rescinded. AYES: Westrick, Smith, Horn, Kline, Babel, Biebuyck. NAYS: Reichle. ABSENT: None. RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED. NB 2 – Water and Sewer Rate Increase East China Charter Township Official Board Minutes November 10, 2025 Trustee Reichle, supported by Treasurer Horn, moved to postpone the water and sewer rate increase to the next meeting on November 17, 2025. Carried. This will require $1.2 Million dollars from the General Fund Balance to subsidize these rates effective January 1, 2026. The proposed revised rate structure is as follows: • • Ready to Serve water $39.29 (20%)/Rate per 1,000 gallons $9.88 (13.4%) Ready to Serve sewer $44.92 (20%)/Rate per 1,000 gallons $7.01 (20%) ADJOURN – Trustee Reichle, supported by Clerk Smith, moved to adjourn at 9:50 p.m. Carried. Sandra Smith, Clerk Verne Westrick, Supervisor

This meeting is open to all members of the public under Michigan’s Open Meetings Act. Persons with disabilities who need accommodations to participate in this meeting should contact the Township Clerk’s Office at 517-546-2817 at least two (2) business days prior to the meeting. Public Hearings. All public hearings must be held as part of a regular or special meeting of the Zoning Board of Appeals. The following rules of procedure shall apply to public hearings held by the Zoning Board of Appeals: 1. Chairperson opens the public hearing and announces the subject. 2. Chairperson summarizes the procedures/rules to be followed during the hearing. 3. Township staff summarizes the application. 4. Applicant presents the main points of the application. 5. Persons having comments on the application are recognized. 6. Chairperson closes the public hearing and returns to the regular/special meeting. 7. Township consultants (if any) present their report and recommendation. 8. Zoning Board members begin deliberations and arrive at a decision. To ensure everyone has the opportunity to speak, the Chairperson may elect to limit the time permitted for each person to speak, except that the applicant may be permitted additional time as the Chairperson allows. The Chairperson may also elect to allow persons to speak only once, until all persons have had the opportunity to speak, at which time the Chairperson, in his/her discretion, may permit additional comments. All comments by the public, staff, and the Zoning Board shall be directed to the Chairperson. All comments shall be related to the request; unrelated comments shall be ruled out of order. A written notice containing the decision of the Zoning Board of Appeals will be sent to petitioners and originators of the request. Public Hearing: Bachman Trust, PZBA2026-02, Parcel #s: 4706-24-100-013, 4706-24-100-011 Article VI SFR – Single Family Residential, Section 6.06 – Dimensional Requirements Except as Otherwise Specified in this Ordinance: Variance request to create a parcel with less than 120 feet of lot width / road frontage Chairman Frenger opened the public hearing and read the instructions. Dan Davenport 6870 Grand River, Brighton, Michigan 48814 for the Bachman Trust requested that the property be split into 8 parcels. The parent parcel was purchased in 1956. Proposed parcel #1 has road access at the intersection of Monterey Court and Edgemont Drive. The existing width (54.27 feet) of Public Road frontage can support a driveway for a single-family residence. Driveway Site distance has been approved by Livingston County Road Commission. The 66 feet width of the parcel is not the width of the public road frontage. The split into individual parcels still requires review and approval by the Township Planning Commissioners. Call to the Public: David Dean Wade 800 East Allen Road – Email No Objection Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft Davita J. Finley 2467 Fisher Road -Handwritten note on Notice of Public Hearing letter in opposition to the request Staff Report Finding of Facts The Ordinance currently requires the following: • Section 26.02-C: The required minimum area and road frontage for each lot, parcel, or site area shall be equal to the minimum lot or parcel width as required in each zoning district. • As shown in the zoning map, these parcels are in the Single- F a m i l y Residential • Zoning District. Section 6.06-C: Minimum of 120 feet for a one (1) acre or more parcel and a minimum of 70 feet for 10,000 square feet to less than (1) acre parcel. As proposed, parcel 1 is a 13.19-acre parcel with 1.75 acres of upland area and would have, according to the survey, 54.27 feet of road frontage, meeting neither the 120-foot nor the 70-foot requirement for Single Family Residential parcels: The Township has historically read the deﬁnition of Building Setback Line to mean that a structure cannot be built on a parcel unless it is sited on the property outside of the parcel setbacks and meets the building setback line standard of the Zoning Ordinance. It is common for parcels in the Township to not have the required road frontage required in the Ordinance. An example of this is a parcel that does not have road frontage, but has an easement for ingress and egress, which is usually at most 66 feet wide, but is usually less. Another nearby example is a parcel that is a ﬂag Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft lot, which has a tail of property connecting the larger portion of the parcel to Fisher Road that is approximately 20 feet wide for their driveway, but which structure meets the property setbacks and the building setback line requirements. While the applicant also raises the deﬁnition of Lot, Waterfront in defense of the request, this deﬁnition does not apply to this request due to the deﬁnitions of Lot, and Lot of Record, because Parcel 1 does not yet exist and is therefore not a Lot of Record. Deﬁnitions: • Building Setback Line: The line formed by the outer surface of a structure or enclosure wall at or with the ﬁnish grade or surface of the ground; pertaining to and deﬁning those minimum (building) setback lines which are established, in general, parallel to the front road right-of-way line and within which setback area no part of a building shall project or be located, except as otherwise provided for by this Ordinance. • Building Line: A line formed by the face of the building, and for the purposes of this Ordinance, a minimum building line is the same as the front setback line. • Lot: A portion of land divided in conformance with all of the provisions of Public Act 288 of 1967 in accordance with Public Act 288 Land Division Act of 1967 as amended, Subdivision Control Act and the Subdivision Regulations of Howell Township. • Lot of Record: A lot existing prior to the adoption of this Ordinance and recorded in the office of the County Register of Deeds. For the purposes of this Ordinance, land contracts and purchase options not recorded in the County Register of Deeds’ Office but dated and executed prior to the effective date of the Ordinance shall also constitute a “lot of record”. (Includes “Parcel of Record”) • Lot, Waterfront: A lot having a frontage directly upon a lake, river or other reasonably sized impoundment of water. The portion adjacent to the water shall be designated as the lake frontage of the lot, and the opposite side shall be designated the road frontage of the lot. • Road Frontage: The legal line of demarcation between a dedicated road right-of-way or easement and abutting land. • Road Line: The line which forms the outer limits of a road right-of-way or easement, and which forms the line from which all road setbacks and front yards are measured. Zoning Ordinance Standards For the ZBA to approve a dimensional variance the applicant must demonstrate a practical difficulty. The ZBA should review the documents submitted by the applicant supporting the variance request against the provisions of the Ordinance, Section 22.07: 1. That special conditions and circumstances exist which are peculiar to the land use, land, structure or building in the same zoning district. • Parcel 4706-24-100-013 is an odd shape, including a road stub off Edgemont Drive. It appears that a much larger development was anticipated that would extend Edgemont Drive through the existing parcel to Pineway Trail allowing for more parcels and more homes to be built. The proposed lot is also an odd shape. While the proposed parcel may not meet the strict letter of the Ordinance, it meets the Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft spirit of the Ordinance by providing access to a public road no less than 20 feet in width, as required by Section 26.03 and 26.13. 2. That literal interpretation of the provisions of this Ordinance would deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties in the same zoning district under the provisions of this Ordinance. • As stated above, there are a lot of parcels in the Township that have no road frontage, only an easement, or have less than the building setback line frontage as road frontage but still have the required access to a public road. 3. That granting of the variance requested will not confer on the applicant any special privilege that is denied by the provisions of this Ordinance to other lands, structures, or buildings in the same zoning district. • It is common in the Township for property to have less than the building setback line amount of road frontage. 4. That no nonconforming uses of other lands, structures, or buildings in the same zoning district, and not permitted use of lands, structures or buildings in other zoning districts, shall be considered grounds for the issuance of a variance. 5. Applicants shall also follow the outline of requirements prescribed by the Zoning Board of Appeals when applying for an appeal for an interpretation of or a variance from the provisions or requirements of this Zoning Ordinance. 6. Reasons set forth in the application justify the granting of the variance, and the variance is the minimum variance that will make possible the reasonable use of the land, building, or structure in the zoning district in which it is located. • The road stub from Edgemont Drive already exists and is over 20’ wide which is enough for access for a single driveway making the request larger than the minimum. 7. The granting of the variance will be in harmony with the general purpose and intent of this Ordinance, and will not be injurious or otherwise detrimental to the public welfare of the zoning district in which it is to be located. • One additional residential driveway on Edgemont Drive will be in harmony with the Ordinance and will not be detrimental to any existing property or owners in this residential area. Respectfully submitted, Jonathan Hohenstein Howell Township Zoning Administrator Motion by Counts, Second by Weaver, “I move that the Zoning Board of Appeals approve the request of Dan Davenport, on behalf of the Bachman Trust, for a dimensional variance from Sections 6.06(C) and 26.02(C) of the Zoning Ordinance to permit proposed Parcel 1, to be split from Parcel No. 4706-24-100-013, to have 54.27 feet of road frontage where 120 feet is required in the ordinance, with access to Edgemont Drive provided by an exclusive private driveway easement, based on the application materials, the Zoning Administrator’s staff report, and the testimony and evidence presented at the hearing, for the following reasons: The Applicant has demonstrated a practical difficulty because, due to the irregular shape of the parent parcel and proposed Parcel 1, including the existing road stub off Edgemont Drive, the width Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft of proposed Parcel 1 is not located along its public road frontage, making strict compliance with the road frontage requirement of Section 26.02(C) unnecessarily burdensome. In compliance with Section 22.07(A), the applicant has shown that there are special conditions and circumstances associated with the irregular shape of the parent parcel and proposed Parcel 1, including the existing road stub off Edgemont Drive, within the Single-Family Residential District that make it difficult to comply with Section 26.02 of the Zoning Ordinance. In compliance with Section 22.07(A)(2), applicant has shown that the literal interpretation of the ordinance would deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties in the Single Family Residential District because there are other parcels within this district that have no road frontage, only an easement, or have less than the building setback line frontage as road frontage but still have required public road access, example Flagpole Lots. In compliance with Section 22.07(A)(3), the applicant has shown that the granting of the variance will not confer any special privilege that is denied to others within the same zoning district because it is common for properties within the Single-Family Residential to have less than the building setback line amount of road frontage. In compliance with Section 22.07(A)(4), no nonconforming uses of other lands, structures, or buildings in the district, and no permitted uses of lands, structures, or buildings in other zoning districts, have been considered as grounds for the issuance of this variance. In compliance with Section 22.07(B), applicant has followed the outline of requirements prescribed by the Zoning Board of Appeals in applying for this variance. In compliance with Section 22.07(C), subject to the conditions set forth below, the variance is the minimum variance that will make possible the reasonable use of the land in the SFR District because the variance is limited to proposed Parcel 1 and the exclusive driveway easement will be limited in width, which provides access to a public road consistent with Sections 26.03 and 26.13. In compliance with Section 22.07(D), the granting of the variance will be in harmony with the general purpose and intent of the Zoning Ordinance and will not be injurious or otherwise detrimental to the public welfare within the Single Family Residential District because one additional residential driveway on Edgemont Drive has minimal to no impact on the surrounding properties, including the adjoining parcels currently owned by the applicant, and the Livingston County Road Commission has recommended approval.” Roll Call: McEvoy- yes, Weaver- yes, Countsyes, Frenger- yes, Williams- yes. Motion passed (5-0). B. Jason Howe, PZBA2026-03, Parcel #: 4706-01-200-022 Article XIV- Supplemental Regulations, Section 14.07- Accessory Structures: Variance request to exceed the maximum square footage for an accessory building on a parcel less than 20 acres in size, as well as a dimensional variance to allow the accessory building to be located in front of the rear line of the property. Steve Brock, presented for Jason Howe, who was present but ill, not allowing him to speak easily. Mr. Howe owns 18.76 acres of land. With the passing of his father Mr. Howe has inherited several large pieces of agricultural pieces of equipment. Therefore, he desires to construct an accessory building to store these pieces of equipment. The dimensions of the building are 40 feet by 80 feet with a square footage of 3,200 feet. This is more than 3,000 square feet specified in the ordinance. There are 2 chicken coops, and a garage which places the square footage in excess by 2,009 square feet. Alternatives of attaching the garage and making chicken coups are not structural but found not to be feasible. Discussion Centered on the position of the accessory building. This was determined by geography and avoidance of proximity to power lines. (Not High voltage power lines). The position of the building made sense with respect to the topography of the property ZBA then focused on the size of accessory building with respect to the parcel size 18.76 acres. Matt Counts pointed out 3,000 square foot buildings were different from 3,000 square foot buildings on 20 acres. Discussion of the issue of whether this ordinance made sense. This was tabled to discuss after the Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft deliberation. Call to Public: None Staff Report Applicant: Jason Howe Property: 5937 Fisher Rd., Howell, MI 48855. Parcel# 4706-01-200-022 Request The owner of the property would like to construct a 3,200 square foot barn to house vehicles, and farm equipment located four feet in front of the rear line of the house. Background Jason Howe purchased the property in 2011. The parcel is approximately 18.76 acres and is located in the Agricultural Residential (AR) zoning district on the corner of Fisher Road and East Allen Road. Howell Township ZBA Meeting Minutes 10/20/2026 Draft Findings of Fact Variance #1 Jason is requesting to construct an accessory structure that exceeds the square footage permitted under the Ordinance. The Ordinance currently limits the maximum square footage of Accessory buildings on parcels with less than 20 acres in the Agricultural Residential zoning district to 3,000 square feet. Section 14.07 C: Accessory Buildings located on lots and parcels in all Zoning Districts shall be subject to the following regulations: Jason’s proposed structure meets the definition of a detached accessory structure (see definition below), since it is not attached to the main house and will be used to store cars and farm equipment. It would be subject to the maximum square footage allowed of 3,000 square feet of accessory structures or 4% of lot area. Historically the Township has used the more restrictive regulation. There are currently four small accessory structures that total approximately 337 square feet and a detached garage that is 1,472 square feet for a total of 1,809 square feet of current accessory structures. Jason’s drawings indicate that the proposed accessory structure is 80’ x 40’ or 3,200 square feet. Jason’s application indicates he is asking for a 1,136 square foot variance but our calculations indicate it would be a 2,009 square foot variance that would be required. Building, Accessory. A supplementary building or structure on the same lot or parcel of land as the main building or buildings or part of the main building occupied by or devoted exclusively to any accessory use; but such use shall not include any building used for dwelling, residential or lodging purposes, or sleeping quarters for human beings except for these dwellings or residential buildings specifically permitted in this ordinance. Variance #2 Jason is also asking for a variance to allow the structure to be located four feet in front of the rear line of the principal dwelling. Section 14.07 B: Detached accessory buildings and structures shall be located entirely in the rear yard outside of the rear setback… There are exceptions to the rule, but they do not apply to this request. Meeting Location: 5151 Marsh Road, Okemos, Ml 48864 Township Hall Providing a safe and welcoming, sustainable, prime community. 9.A CONSENT AGENDA BOARD COMMUNICATIONS Outlook Meridian Township Clerk’s Office to Begin Early Voting on October 24 Press Release From Samantha Diehl <diehl@meridian.mi.us> Date Wed 10/21/2026 1:31 PM To Samantha Diehl <diehl@meridian.mi.us> 1 attachment (15 MB) Meridian Township Early Voting (1).jpg; FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 21, 2026 CONTACT: Angela Demas, Township Clerk 517.853.4304 | demas@meridian.mi.us Meridian Township Clerk’s Office to Begin Early Voting on October 24 Nine Consecutive Days of Early Voting Available for November 3 General Election Meridian Township, Mich., – Before the November 3 General Election, registered voters in Meridian Township will have the opportunity to vote early at the designated early voting site. Qualified voters have the option to vote early in person beginning on Saturday, October 24, through Sunday, November 1. The early voting site is located in the Town Hall Room of the Meridian Township Municipal Building (5151 Marsh Road, Okemos) and is open from 9:00 am to 5:00 pm each day. The Clerk’s Office will also be open from 9:00 am to 5:00 pm on Saturday, October 31, and Sunday, November 1, to assist residents. An early voting site operates similarly to a polling location that voters would use on Election Day. Eligible voters during early voting will be issued a ballot to cast their vote and insert it into the tabulator at the early voting site. Anyone voting by absentee ballot can also cast their ballot at the early voting site. To check voter registration status, visit michigan.gov/vote. For questions about the general election, please contact the Meridian Township Clerk’s Office at 517.853.4300 or clerksoffice@meridian.mi.us. Additional information can also be found online at meridian.mi.us/elections. ### Samantha Diehl Communications Manager diehl@meridian.mi.us W 517.853.4378 5151 Marsh Road | Okemos, MI 48864 meridian.mi.us FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE October 19, 2026 CONTACT: Emma Campbell, Land Stewardship Coordinator 517.853.4600 | ecampbell@meridian.mi.us Meridian Township Earns ‘Bird City Michigan’ Designation Township Joins 11 Other Bird City Communities in Michigan Meridian Township, Mich., – By demonstrating its commitment to creating healthy bird habitats and advancing local conservation efforts, Meridian Township has officially been designated a Bird City Michigan community, joining 11 other communities across the state recognized for their bird-friendly practices. Launched by Michigan Audubon in 2025, with founding partner Ford Motor Company, Bird City Michigan is a science-based program that recognizes communities for taking meaningful action to protect birds and their habitats. The program is part of the international Bird City Network and encourages municipalities, conservation organizations, and residents to work together to create healthier environments for both birds and people. “We are beyond proud to earn this designation through our current stewardship efforts, which take place all year round with dedicated staff and volunteers. Reducing bird-window collisions at Township buildings and continuing to restore native plant populations is our main goal to help local birds thrive,” said Land Stewardship Coordinator Emma Campbell. Meridian Township earned the designation through its ongoing efforts to preserve natural areas, enhance wildlife habitat, promote environmental stewardship, and engage the community in conservation initiatives. The Township's application highlighted local programs and partnerships that support habitat protection, environmental education, and sustainable land management. “Michigan Audubon is especially proud to welcome the Township as a Bird City Michigan community. While our reach is statewide, our headquarters are located right here in Meridian Township. The collaboration among the Township's staff and volunteers exemplifies a community creating spaces where both wildlife and people can thrive,” said Linda Smith, Director of Partnerships for Michigan Audubon. Michigan Audubon connects birds and people for the benefit of both through conservation, education, and research across Michigan. Incorporated in 1905, the organization stewards more than 4,000 acres of habitat at 20 bird sanctuaries throughout the state. For more information, contact Michigan Audubon at birdcity@michiganaudubon.org. The Bird City Michigan-Meridian Township team included Township staff, the Meridian Green Team, the Meridian Township Environmental Commission, the Harris Nature Center, the Meridian Conservation Corps (MCC), and the Capital Area Audubon Society. Together, the team completed the application process and identified opportunities to further support bird conservation efforts within the community. -more- The community of Meridian Township is in close proximity to the Michigan State Capitol and Michigan State University. The Township serves the community through exceptional services, beneficial amenities and an outstanding quality of life. It is a welcoming community that celebrates quality education, recreation and lifestyles. OXFORD ROAD, OXFORD, MI 48371 2) RESPECTS TO THE FLAG 3) ROLL CALL 4) APPROVAL OF AGENDA 5) CONFLICTS OF INTEREST/EX-PARTE CONTACT 6) APPROVAL OF MINUTES A. 9-24-2026, Planning Commission Regular Meeting Minutes 7) PUBLIC COMMENTS 8) PUBLIC HEARING(S) A. Zoning Ordinance Text Amendments to: • Update Article 2, Section 2.2, of the Township of Oxford Zoning Ordinance, to establish a definition of “Data Center” and provide regulations for large-scale data processing, computer server, data storage, telecommunications equipment, cryptocurrency data mining, and associated infrastructure uses. These facilities are used for the processing, storage, and transmission of digital information and may include supporting infrastructure such as backup power generation, cooling systems, fuel storage, and security systems. • Update Article 10, Section 10.1.H., 10.1.J and 10.1.K, to modify electromagnetic interference, noise and vibration standards for all uses in the Township. These standards will be applicable to data centers as well as all other uses in the Township. • Update Article 3, Section 3.5, to make data centers a special land use in the Data Center Overlay District (DCO). This overlay has been applied to Light Industrial (I-1) and General Industrial (I-2) zoned parcels north of Hummer Lake Road and south of Xcelsior Drive, and between Xcelsior Drive and M-24. The Data Center Overlay (DCO) is an overlay designation and does not replace the underlying zoning district. Data centers may be considered as special land uses only on property within the DCO that is also zoning I-1 or I-2, subject to Section 5.41. • Add a new section to Article 5, Section 5.41. This section addresses required noise studies, cooling system design, anticipated utility demand and capacity verification, traffic analysis, screening and sound barrier standards, security measures, backup power generation and fuel storage, decommissioning plans, development agreements, impact assessments, public service training and equipment requirements, setbacks, renewable energy requirements, thermal emission standards, annual reports requirements, architectural standards, and performance violations and remedies. • Update Article 4, Section 4.7, to clarify the process under which a special land use permit may be suspended or revoked by the Township Board of Trustees for all special land uses in the Township. • Add Appendix A to the zoning ordinance. The appendix is titled “Oxford Township Data Center Engineering Requirements” and provides required information, designs, and standards relating to municipal water supply and sewer, water supply for cooling, water recycling, water discharge, hydrology, stormwater management, traffic and site access, ground wells, environmental impact assessments, and construction planning as it relates to data centers. • Add Appendix B to the zoning ordinance. The appendix is titled “Oxford Township Fire Department Data Center Fire and Life Safety Review Requirements” and provides required information, designs, and standards relating to fire protection systems, water supply, battery energy storage systems, backup power generation and fuel storage, emergency access and site operations, pre-incident planning, and emergency coordination as it relates to data centers. B. Consideration of a Zoning Map Amendment to establish a Data Center Overlay District (DCO) on all properties zoned Light Industrial (I-1) and General Industrial (I-2) located along Xcelsior Drive, Hummer Lake Road, Metamora Road (between Hummer Lake Road and M-24) and M-24 (between Hummer Lake Road and Metamora Road). The purpose of the proposed Data Center Overlay District would be to allow data centers as a special land use on these parcels. 9) UNFINISHED BUSINESS 10) NEW BUSINESS 11) COMMUNICATIONS AND/OR COMMITTEE REPORTS 12) PLANNER/ENGINEER REPORTS A. Sharpe Activity Report will be available at the next Planning Commission regular meeting. On September 10th, 2026, the Planning Commission conducted a public hearing on the initial draft of the data center text and map amendments to the zoning ordinance. Per public comment and Planning Commission deliberations, it was decided that another public hearing was necessary to outline all the changes that have been proposed to original draft data center zoning ordinance and map. This memo provides a summary of all changes made to the draft ordinance and map amendment, as well as what section and page number those changes can be found. Both the CLEAN and REDLINE version are provided in the packet. PLEASE NOTE, page numbers used in this memo coincide with the REDLINE version of the proposed ordinance. Included in the packet is a full size and zoomed in version of the proposed zoning map showing the new overlay district. A satellite aerial image and sample of the zoning map showing the 300foot buffer from residential, institutional, or recreational zoned or used properties are also included. The buffer is shown in purple. Staff reviewed the following materials to provide guidance on the proposed changes to be presented at the November 16th, 2026 public hearing: • All public comment included in the packet of the September 10th, 2026 public hearing. • All public and Planning Commissioner comments verbalized during the September 10th, 2026, public hearing. • All printed materials left for the Planning Commission during the September 10th, 2026, public hearing. • All emails sent to the Township, as well as any attachments regarding data centers. • All mail sent to the Township regarding data centers. • Several other community data center ordinances including, but not limited to: o Brandon Township o Howell Township Benjamin R. Carlisle, President John L. Enos, Vice President Douglas J. Lewan, Principal David Scurto, Principal Sally M. Elmiger, Principal R. Donald Wortman, Principal Craig Strong, Principal Paul Montagno, Principal Megan Masson-Minock, Principal Laura Kreps, Principal Richard K. Carlisle, Past President/Senior Principal October 27th, 2026 Public Hearing for Revised Data Center Text and Map Zoning Amendments • o Dexter Township o Washington Township o Pittsfield Township The Michigan Township Association’s model data center ordinance. This research was conducted in tandem with the Township Engineer, Attorney, Fire Department, and Building Department. These departments and/or consultants have reviewed and approved of the proposed text and map amendments presented in the packet. One important item to consider is that not all the areas of concern (i.e. emissions, well water use and discharge, electrical consumption, electrical rates, etc.) fall under the Township’s authority to regulate. Whether or not the proposed ordinance specifically calls for the approval from these other agencies, that approval is required. Proof of third-party approvals is required as part of the Township’s site plan review process. The Township can hire expert consultants to review the validity of such approved permits if it deems necessary. The cost of these services is borne by the data center applicant and/or operator. After hearing public comments and conducting deliberations, the Planning Commission may take one of the following steps: • Motion to send the draft ordinance text and zoning map amendments to the Township Board with the recommendation that the Board adopt the proposed changes. • Motion to send the draft ordinance text and zoning map amendments to the Township Board with the recommendation that the Board adopt the proposed amendments with the condition that the minor changes discussed during the meeting be incorporated into the draft amendments. • Motion to send the draft ordinance text and zoning map amendments back to staff for major revisions based on the meeting’s discussion. Should the draft text and map amendments be sent to the Township Board, they will require a first and second reading during two separate regular Board meetings. Once the proposed amendments have been sent to the Board, the Board has the authority to request changes to the ordinance without sending them back to the Planning Commission. Please note the moratorium on accepting and reviewing an application to build or operate a data center in the Township expires February 11th, 2027. Thank you for your time. Respectfully, October 27th, 2026 Public Hearing for Revised Data Center Text and Map Zoning Amendments Summarized Changes to the Draft Ordinance Text and Zoning Map Amendments Zoning Map Overlay (Specific to Data Centers) • Reduced size of Overlay district for Data Centers on the zoning map. Original Overlay September 10th Meeting Overlay Proposal New Overlay November 16th Meeting Overlay Proposal Appendix A / Appendix B Format (Specific to Data Centers) • In the original format of the proposed ordinance, the Oxford Township Data Center Engineering Requirements and Oxford Township Fire Department Data Center Fire and Life Safety Review Requirements documents were separate from the ordinance. This was meant to allow these documents to be updated in a more efficient timeline to keep pace with the evolving technology associated with these uses. Upon further conversations with the Township Attorney, it was decided that these requirements are more enforceable and/or defensible as part of the ordinance and not stand-alone documents. For that reason, they are now appendices to the zoning ordinance and will require zoning ordinance text amendments to modify. Appendix A (Specific to Data Centers) • Facilities must demonstrate use of best practices and best available technology for energy conservation. Pg. 1 • Outlined process for a data center to apply to connect to the Township water/sewer district. Pg. 1 October 27th, 2026 Public Hearing for Revised Data Center Text and Map Zoning Amendments • • • • • • • • • • • • Cooling systems must be closed loop with no routine discharging to the municipal sewer. Cooling systems must use at least 50% non-potable water and R744 refrigerant. Pg 1 Data Center must outline protocols it will enact during drought conditions. The Township may review the water meter to ensure compliance with drought protocols. Pg. 2 Access to the municipal sewer shall only be for non-cooling discharge and only if there is sufficient capacity in the system to accommodate the data center. Pg 2 Water reuse and/or onsite treatment and ground discharge plans are required. Pg 2 EGLE must review the hydrology study. Pg 3 The radius for well analysis has increased from 2,000 feet to one mile. Pg 3 & 4 The Township may require supplemental information not outlined in the ordinance to ensure compliance with design standards. Pg. 4 Traffic and site access now includes the same standards used to regulate gravel mining and hauling operations as outlined in the zoning ordinance Section 5.25. Pg. 5 Water Use Effectiveness metrics are required as part of annual reporting. Pg 6 Groundwater Monitoring Wells are required before and after construction of the data center to establish baseline water levels and monitor levels during operations. Pg. 6 The Environmental Impact Assessment now requires a report from a licensed environmental engineer outlining expected impacts of the data center on the environment, wildlife, and natural resources in the surrounding area. Pg. 6 A construction plan is now required to outline the timeline and process for constructing the data center. Pg. 7 Appendix B (Specific to Data Centers) • Battery systems shall comply with NFPA 855. Pg 1 • The hazard mitigation analysis now requires demonstration of no thermal propagation under UL 9540A. Pg. 1 • A description of emergency shutdown procedures is now required. Pg. 2 • A detailed evaluation of any risk of intentional or inadvertent chemical or hazardous material discharge is now required. Pg. 2 • Walkthroughs with the Fire Department are required at least once a year. Pg 2 Article 2 Definitions (Specific to Data Centers) • Updated data center definition to include other similar uses. Pg. 2 Article 3 Zoning District Regulations (Specific to Data Centers) • Section 3.5 – Clarified that Data Centers within the Data Center Overlay must comply with the underlying zone designation standards if not specifically outlined elsewhere in the Ordinance. Pg. 2 • Section 4.7 – Clarified the process for suspending or revoking a special land use permit for all uses in the Township. To provide for the adoption of supplementary rules and regulations and other matters related to the museum facilities owned by the Charter Township of Port Huron. Section 1. Title This Ordinance shall be known as the “Port Huron Charter Township Historical Commission Ordinance.” Section 2. Purpose The purpose of this Ordinance is to provide for the use, protection, regulation and control of the Museum facilities, areas, and other matters concerning historical preservation, education, and conservation. To provide for the adoption of supplementary rules and regulations and other matters related to the museum facilities owned by the Charter Township of Port Huron. Section 3. Establishment The Port Huron Charter Township Historical Commission is hereby established. Section 4. Membership The Historical Commission shall consist of five (5) members who shall be appointed by the Supervisor with the approval of the Township Board. Not more than two members may be Township Board members. Each member shall serve a term of 3 years. Historical Commission Members and volunteers are expected to follow the “Committee, Commission, & Board Commitment Standards” as established October 7, 2013 and the Historical Commission Agreement & Code of Ethics. Letters of interest of appointment as well as letters of resignation shall both be directed to the Township Supervisor. (Questionnaire located on Township Website) Section 5. Grounds for Removal Any member that violates the “Committee, Commission, & Board Commitment Standards and/or the Historical Commission Agreement & Code of Ethics may be removed from their seat on the Historical Commission by majority vote of the Township Board. Section 6. Officers, Meetings & Records A. The Historical Commission shall organize by annually electing a Chairperson, Vice Chairperson, Recording Secretary/Treasurer, and any other officers from its membership as it may deem necessary.

ROLL CALL Supervisor Johnson, Clerk Feraco, Treasurer Davis, Trustee Meinke, Trustee Hoskins, Trustee McKay, Trustee Blanchard 7-PRESENT 4. Supervisor Report- Supervisor Johnson discussed the need for a new lawnmower and stated that he would obtain multiple quotes for board consideration at the November meeting. 5. Clerk Report-Clerk Feraco announced that voter information guides were available and reminded residents that early voting runs October 24 through November 1, with Election Day on November 3, 2026. 6. Treasurer Report- Treasurer Davis reported on investment earnings and offered to review the distribution of collected tax revenues with interested residents. 7. Moved by Treasurer Davis, Supported by Trustee Blanchard to APPROVE OF AGENDA (Additions, Subtractions, Corrections) Roll Call- 7-YES 0-NO MOTION CARRIED 8. PUBLIC COMMENTS ON AGENDA- A resident raised concerns regarding potential blight and property maintenance in the Valhalla/Val Heights area. Questions included whether chickens may roam onto neighboring properties, unlicensed or apparently abandoned vehicles, and overgrown lawns or outdoor furniture/appliances. Township officials clarified that chickens must remain on the owner’s property, such conditions may constitute blight, and residents should submit complaints for enforcement. The resident also asked about the timeframe for addressing unlicensed vehicles and noted concerns regarding the recent absence of the Township’s blight control officer. A resident requested that the Township develop a contingency plan for future personnel or service issues, citing concerns regarding the prolonged placement of a refrigerator along a roadway as a safety and neighborhood concern. A resident questioned the status and accuracy of the September 8 meeting minutes and the process used to prepare them. The resident also expressed concerns regarding the budget workshop, including the lack of detailed financial information and planning, and asked whether board-issued cell phones and related expenses would be included in the 2027 budget. The resident also reminded the Board to account for the purchase of flag holders and encouraged a more "Neighbors Serving Neighbors" organized budget process. A resident expressed concerns regarding Township-issued cell phones and the handling of blight complaints, including anonymous complaints. The resident also discussed a pending FOIA appeal, citing delays and concerns that the records provided were incomplete or duplicative, and requested that the Board proceed with scheduling the appeal. 9. Moved by Treasurer Davis, Supported by Trustee Meinke to APPROVE OF CONSENT AGENDA ITEMS: Minutes of September 28th Payment of bills in the amount $92,576.27 Budget Report 2026 BCPD and Bedford Charter Twp Fire Department Reports Building and Zoning Report Assessor Report- Planning Commission Liaison Report Payment of Bills for August Roll Call 7-YES 0-NO MOTION CARRIED ZTO™MOO Dp 10. REPORTS Police & Fire-Officer Phillips reported that police calls for service had decreased, including assault-related calls. He provided clarification regarding animal-control enforcement and noted that ordinance language is being reviewed for accuracy and consistency. He also stated that animal and livestock complaints would be addressed as appropriate. Fire-Lieutenant Curtis Lundberg reported 97 calls for service in September, approximately 72% of which were medical. He also noted a motor vehicle accident involving a residence and stated that the individual who fled the scene was apprehended. The department has responded to 941 calls year-to-date. The annual spaghetti dinner was announced for Saturday at the Lions Club. Assessor Michele reported that she is becoming familiar with the new assessment system and continues to complete field work, review building permits, and prepare for the 2027 assessment roll. She noted that disabled veteran exemptions may carry forward annually when eligible and that residential land values continue to increase. She also provided information regarding taxable value uncapping and frequently asked assessment questions. Road report- Mike Staib(Team: Johnson, Hires, Staib and McCarty) Mike Staib reported on a meeting with the County regarding the proposed five-year road maintenance plan. He noted concerns with chip-seal effectiveness and recommended greater coordination, prioritization of problem areas, and consideration of alternative maintenance methods. He also reported reviewing "Neighbors Serving Neighbors" township roads and developing a list of priority areas for discussion with the County. Parks & Rec Toni Ardis McPeak reported that the festival was canceled due to ADA compliance issues following playground equipment removal and clarified that the cancellation was not related to excluding religious or disability organizations. She expressed concerns regarding communication, Parks and Recreation funding, park maintenance priorities, and the proposed pickleball courts. She also reported that the Parks and Recreation Committee plans to reassess priorities, update the master plan, and evaluate the needs of each park. [Vote of 7-0, 7 in favor, 0 opposed.] Ms. Carroll expressed concern that the adjacent property has been farmed in soybeans or corn for more than two decades and stated her opposition to introducing commercial storage uses in an agricultural area due to expected noise and traffic impacts. Mr. Fedewa spoke in support of the zoning text amendment, noting it was pursued at the recommendation of the former interim Planning Director to avoid concerns about spot zoning. He clarified that the amendment would apply only to parcels in the Highway Overlay District and highlighted that A2 zoning already allows many non-agricultural special land uses. He stated that locally owned storage facilities place minimal demand on public services while generating significant tax revenue and added that the parcels in Page | 5 question are small, not actively farmed, and not viable for agricultural production. Ms. Wood, spoke in opposition to the proposed commercial development, citing concerns about increased traffic and resident safety, and stated that other neighbors would likely oppose the project if informed. Stephanie Schafer moved to close the public hearing, supported by Zach Rudat. Motion carried unanimously. [Vote of 7-0, 7 in favor, 0 opposed.] The Commission found that no evidence was presented demonstrating changed conditions or demographic or economic shifts to justify the petition. The Future Land Use Map was noted as a guiding document rather than a regulatory component of the zoning ordinance, no error in judgment was made as it relates to this land use. The Commission expressed concern that establishing a precedent could allow the identified special land use more broadly within the A2 district. Potential impacts on public services and facilities were reviewed. Effects on surrounding rural residential property values were considered but could not be determined definitively. The petition was found not to comply with the County’s Comprehensive Plan. Environmental impacts, including drainage, wastewater, water quality, and natural resources, were also evaluated. Lyman Planning Department (517) 323-8560 To: Delta Township Planning Commission From: Peter Menser, Planning & Economic Development Director Date: November 2, 2026 Subject: Special Land Use Permit #PSL2026-0005 (Michiana Land Investment, LLC), establish a planned unit development (PUD) for the proposed 63-lot Echo Valley East residential development located east of S. Canal Rd., north of W. Mt. Hope Hwy. on Blue Ridge Dr. (Parcel #040-022-300-083-00). Applicant Michiana Land Investment, LLC has submitted a Special Land Use Permit (SLUP) application to establish a planned unit development (PUD) for the proposed Echo Valley East residential development. Echo Valley East as proposed would be a single-family detached site condominium development comprised of 63 lots on 30.16 acres. The property is zoned RB (Single-Family - Low Density). The requested PUD would allow for a reduction in lot size, lot coverage, and building setbacks in exchange for the preservation of at least 25 percent of the total site as open space. This project originally received SLUP approval from the Township Board on October 17, 2022. The Planning Commission granted Site Plan Review approval on May 8, 2023, followed by final staff approval on July 18, 2023. The Site Plan Review approval expired July 18, 2025, and a one-year extension was granted by the Zoning Administrator, which ran until July 18, 2026, when it expired. The approved SLUP expired along with the Site Plan Review approval. SLUP Process The Special Land Use Permit process consists of two phases, a public hearing at the Planning Commission followed by review of the project by the Delta Township Board. For a SLUP, the Planning Commission is advisory to the Board, it will provide a recommendation on the request, with the Board granting final approval. If SLUP approval is granted by the Township Board, the project still must receive Site Plan Review approval prior to moving ahead to building and trades permit applications. The applicant has indicated they will apply for that process following a decision on the SLUP application. Surrounding Zoning and Land Uses North: RB (Single Family - Low Density), Carrier Creek Drain District, Interstate 496 South: RB (Single Family - Low Density), Echo Valley platted subdivision East: RB (Single Family - Low Density), AG-2 (Agricultural/Residential), single family dwellings West: RB (Single Family - Low Density), Echo Valley platted subdivision MOTION AGENDA Echo Valley East PUD (Michiana Land Investment, LLC) Planning Commission (November 9, 2026) Page 2 Zoning A PUD allows a developer to provide the same number of dwellings as permitted in the underlying zoning district, but on smaller lots and with reduced setbacks and lot coverage. The following illustrates the differences between RB zoning standards to those allowed in a RB-zoned PUD: Zoning Standard Permitted Uses Min. Lot Area Min. Lot Width/Frontage Max Lot Coverage Front yard setback Side yard setback Rear yard setback Max. bldg. height Max Density (du/a, dwelling units per acre) RB Detached single-family dwellings 12,000 sq. ft. 80 ft. 30% 30 ft. 8 ft. 30 ft. 40 ft 3.63 du/a RB - PUD Detached single-family dwellings, attached twofamily dwellings None 60 ft. 40% 24 ft. None None 40 ft. 3.63 du/a Bonus available Open Space A PUD project must provide a minimum of 25 percent of the total site area as open space for passive or active recreation that is equally available for use by all residents in the development. Open space must be conveniently located in relation to dwelling units and have minimum dimensions which are usable for the intended functions. Open spaces may include land that is temporarily or permanently inundated by water. An open space agreement must be established by the developer that ensures preservation and maintenance of the open space areas in perpetuity prior to Site Plan Review approval for the project. For the proposed project, the overall site is 30.2 acres, and the applicant has identified a 7.78-acre open space area consisting of both cleared and uncleared areas and a detention pond on the northern portion of the site, adjacent to the Carrier Creek. The proposed open space is 25.8 percent of the overall site. PUD Density RB zoning allows a maximum project density of 3.63 dwelling units per acre (du/a). The project as proposed has a density of 2.1 du/a. In a PUD, residential density is not permitted to exceed what is typically allowed in the underlying zoning district, however a density bonus is available if a project provides a minimum of 30 percent of the site area as open space. To determine project density, the Zoning Ordinance provides a sliding scale that grants additional density as additional open space is provided. The proposed development has 25.8 percent open space and therefore does not qualify for a density bonus, nor is the applicant seeking one. Echo Valley East PUD (Michiana Land Investment, LLC) Planning Commission (November 9, 2026) Page 3 2026 Non-Motorized Transportation Plan There are no features on or around the project site in the non-motorized transportation plan. An on-road bicycle lanes are present along W. Mt. Hope Hwy., south of the project site. The project does have the required fivefoot-wide sidewalks shown along lots in the proposed development. Streets and Traffic The new streets in the proposed development will be dedicated as public roads and maintained by the Eaton County Road Commission (ECRC). The applicant provided a trip generation analysis prepared by Fleis & Vandenbrink which concludes that the number of trips generated by the proposed development do not meet the threshold for a full traffic study. Floodplain, Wetlands The applicant submitted a wetland delineation report prepared by Rapid Environmental Group (REG). The report identifies three wetlands (Wetlands A, B, and C) in the central portion of the site, but notes that due to size and location, the wetlands are not regulated and therefore can be filled. Floodplain associated with the Carrier Creek drain is present along the north side of the site. No development is proposed in the floodplain. Public Utilities Public utilities (water and sanitary sewer) are located in the vicinity of the subject site and are available to serve the dwellings in the proposed development. The stormwater system is regulated and approved by the Eaton County Drain Commission (EDCD). 2026 Master Plan The subject site is identified as Rural Preserve (RP) on the Future Land Use Map within the 2026 Master Plan. In the Plan, RP is noted as being intended to maintain existing rural or semi-rural character while allowing for thoughtfully planned development. Recommended uses in the RP designation include detached single-family homes, which is the proposed use of the site. The following provides a summary of the proposal’s consistency with the SLUP criteria and the specific ordinance standards for a PUD: SLUP Standards of Approval (Section 7.03) 1. Compatibility with the Comprehensive Plan. The proposed Special Land Use shall be compatible and in accordance with the goals, objectives and policies of the Delta Charter Township Comprehensive Plan and any associated sub-area and corridor plans. Staff comment: The proposed project aligns with the 2026 Master Plan and related Future Land Use Map designation of Rural Preserve. Echo Valley East PUD (Michiana Land Investment, LLC) Planning Commission (November 9, 2026) Page 4 2. Compatibility with Adjacent Uses. The proposed Special Land Use shall be constructed, operated, and maintained so as to be compatible with the existing or intended character of the general vicinity and so as not to change the essential character of the area in which it is proposed. A Special Land Use shall be designed and constructed so as not to create a significant detrimental impact, as compared to the impacts of permitted uses. Staff comment: The proposed development is adjacent to an existing detached single-family home neighborhood named Echo Valley. 3. Impact on Public Services. The proposed Special Land Use shall be served adequately by essential public facilities and services, such as highways, streets, police and fire protection, drainage, water and sewage facilities. Such services shall be provided and accommodated without an unreasonable public burden. Staff comment: Public utilities are available to serve the subject site. Negative impacts to public facilities and services are not expected. 4. Impact on the Overall Environment. The proposed Special Land Use shall not involve uses, activities, processes, materials and equipment, or conditions of operation that will be detrimental to the natural environment, public health, safety, or welfare by reason of excessive production of traffic, noise, smoke, odors, or other such nuisance in comparison to the impacts associated with typical permitted uses. Staff comment: The new facility is not expected to produce excessive traffic, noise, smoke odors, or other such nuisances. 5. Traffic Impact. The proposed Special Land Use shall be located and designed in a manner which will minimize the impact of traffic, taking into consideration: pedestrian access and safety; vehicle trip generation (i.e. volumes); types of traffic, access location and design, circulation and parking design; street and bridge capacity; and traffic operations at nearby intersections and access points. Efforts shall be made to ensure that multiple transportation modes are safely and effectively accommodated to provide alternate modes of access and alleviate vehicular traffic congestion. The applicant shall comply with the Township Complete Street Ordinance. Staff comment: The proposed use will not generate significant traffic beyond those expected in a typical residential development. 6. Operational Characteristics. The nature and character of the activities, processes, materials, equipment, or conditions of operation, either specifically or typically associated with the use shall be reviewed. Staff comment: Negative impacts are not anticipated from the proposed development. 7. Outdoor Operations. Measures shall be taken to ensure that outdoor activity, storage, and work areas will be compatible with adjacent land uses. Staff comment: The proposed use is expected to be compatible with surrounding land uses. Echo Valley East PUD (Michiana Land Investment, LLC) Planning Commission (November 9, 2026) Page 5 8. Compliance with Zoning Ordinance Standards. The proposed Special Land Use shall be designed, constructed, operated, and maintained to meet the stated intent of the zoning district and shall comply with all applicable ordinance standards. Staff comment: The proposed development will meet the RB zoning district standards. 9. Special Land Use Approval Specific Requirements. The general standards and requirements of this Section are basic to all uses authorized by Special Land Use approval. The specific and detailed requirements relating to uses and area requirements must also be satisfied for those uses. Staff comment: The proposed project must meet the nine general Special Land Use Permit criteria listed in Section 7.03 of the zoning ordinance (reviewed above) and the specific standards for a PUD in Section 5.03, which are detailed below. PUD General Standards for Review - Section 5.03 1. The proposed development shall be consistent with, and further the implementation of the Comprehensive Plan or represent land use policies which are a logical and acceptable change in the Comprehensive Plan. Staff comment: The proposed development aligns with the 2026 Master Plan designation of Rural Preserve. 2. The proposed development shall be adequately served by public facilities and services including, but not limited to, streets, sidewalks and pathways, water and sanitary sewer facilities, drainage improvements, and police and fire protection, or the applicant shall confirm that these facilities and services can be provided. Staff comment: The proposed development will be served by public streets, sidewalks, water and sanitary sewer, stormwater system, and police and fire protection. 3. The development shall encourage the provision of useful open spaces and long-term conservation of natural features and resources. Staff comment: A 7.78-acre open space area is provided on the north side of the project site, which will be dedicated to the condo association and preserved in perpetuity. 4. The mix of housing types and densities and the relationship between residential and non-residential uses shall be acceptable in terms of convenience, privacy, and compatibility. Staff comment: No non-residential land uses are proposed. 5. A PUD may … projects including: - Auto Owners training center - Raising Cane's - Horrocks - Eyde rezoning - School zoning amendment - Data centers The next meeting is scheduled for October 12 and there is currently nothing on the agenda.
