NEW BUSINESS Zoning Administrator (Mr. Czyzio): ● Around 1967 a gas station was built at that location. ● I have some documentation that mentions August of 1994 and August of 1995 about Total Petroleum purchasing that property and a letter from the Township stating that the property is currently zoned C2 and that use does fit with that particular zoning classification on that property. 10-5-2026 PC Minutes ● At tonight’s meeting we are looking at a special use permit for the land use. We are not doing a site plan or anything like that. So, the question is, can a gas station go on this particular property? ● I know that the applicant for this particular property has also received approval for some zoning changes from the ZBA for setbacks and what not. That is already complete. So, tonight the main focus is for this hearing and the applicant's request is to make sure he can do the use of a gas station on this particular property. 1. PUBLIC HEARING on Special Use Permit for a First Stop Gas Station at 8490 W. Mt. Morris Rd, Parcel No. 08-02-300-009, pursuant to Article 18 section 36-1800 Special Use Permits OPEN FOR PUBLIC HEARING at 6:06 p.m. Mark Koerner (Attorney from Foster Swift Collin & Smith PC) ● Here on behalf of Rick Hansen ● Statement of Zoning Board of Appeals has approved some variance request. We have not yet received this as of yet and the minutes have not been approved. ● A FOIA request has been requested and did not receive any documentation to that effect. ● Your review of a special use permit application focuses on 3 primary things: the special land use consistent to promote the intent purpose of the ordinances, the purpose will ensure the land use or activity authorized will be compatible with the adjacent uses, natural environment and compacities of public service facilities affected by the proposed use, and the special land use sought is consistent with public health service, safety and welfare. We are here today to indicate that we do not believe that the applicant can satisfy any of those requirements. ● The first is that the ordinances seek and preserve community care or encourage orderly development protecting adjoined properties promote aesthetic development patterns or advanced long-term planning objectives. ● In this case we don’t see how an additional gas station immediately adjacent to one that is already there furthers those goals. Instead, it introduces a commercial use which primary 10-5-2026 PC Minutes function is an accommodation of additional vehicle traffic brought in to service the immediate area. ● The existence of the current gas station located at 8490 W. Mt. Morris Rd further undermines any claim that it satisfies that requirement of the ordinance. ● The Commission may consider if the concentrating of two gas stations in one vicinity would be duplicating an existing service. ● Traffic movement, fuel delivery activity, lighting, signage and impervious surface and petroleum related risk. ● We further believe that the proposed use is not compatible with the adjacent land use of the natural environment. I believe the information was submitted to the Zoning Board of Appeals regarding the study that was conducted by environmental resources June 17, 2026. The Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs of the State of Michigan underground storage tank, indicated that it was a gas station since 1967, four underground storage tanks were removed in July/August 1994 following a confirmed leak of petroleum products. Approximately 53 yards of contaminated soil and 495 gallons of contaminated ground water were reportedly removed with replacement of 2 tenthousand-gallon gasoline tanks. ● This site clearly had contamination. The underground storage tank issue was closed by EGLE. Due to a lapse in time, it was closed. This was a statutory default due to the agency not responding in time. ● There is still currently a tank underground and there are issues with respect to the way that the water pattern flows from a contamination stand point. Additionally, the report identifies additional unresolved exposure pathways. Those are vapor issues and those have not been addressed. So, there are some environmental problems with this property. We have contacted EGLE. There has been no due care obligations undertaken. There has been no baseline of phase 1 environmental assessment occurred or a phase 2 or any base line environmental evaluation that has been filed with the state. ● The well issue is important because there is a requirement by EGLE that the placement of any underground storage tank cannot occur within more than 800 feet of an existing well. There is a well at a church and a residence nearby that we believe are within 100 feet which is another issue. 10-5-2026 PC Minutes ● Ultimately our argument is that the proposed use is not consistent with the public health, safety and welfare. ● The plans that have been submitted show the insistence of a 35-foot fuel tanker that is supposed to go on the property. And if you have been to the property, you can see that its dimensions, it is not a large property and the trail of the pathways and everything else that they have listed on the property that they identify. The method on which they are supposed to bring fuel will only increase traffic, increase number of vehicles and create a public safety risk. ● We also are unaware of any traffic study to show what the impacts of traffic in the area would be with another gas station with two exits and entrances in that area. ● My client also has a signed letter from 200 property owners that are opposed to the redevelopment of this property as an additional gas station. ● Under the Township ordinance it indicates that you are required to approve a special land use if you find the first three requirements are met. It is mandatory and we feel that section D of your ordinance requires approval only when the Commission first determines that the special land use standard has been satisfied. When the record demonstrates noncompliance with section A, B and C the Commission has the authority and the obligation to deny the application. And mandatory approval language is only after compliance has been established. For those reasons we request the special land use application be denied. Tim Hebert (ERG)- I represent Rick on a variety of environmental sites. ● I have about 42 years of experience in environmental containment. ● The biggest concern I have from the environmental standpoint is that there are a lot of due care issues still pending out there. ● As we previously heard, the site itself was closed under default of the State of Michigan. They failed to review the closure file. ● There is contamination both in soil and ground water on the site. The depth of the ground water is about 7 feet below grade. There are records that show that the soil and ground water are contaminated east and west of McKinley Rd. 10-5-2026 PC Minutes ● I don’t believe that thorough evaluation and definition of the assessment activity previously conducted by others defines the extent of contamination. And the biggest issue that really stands out right now is the due care obligations of the new owner. ● By approving the installation of subsurface structures to redevelop a property that has contamination without thoroughly assessing and understanding the extent of the impact is a volitional due care obligation he carries. Which one of them is, he shall not undertake activities to exacerbate the existing conditions of the site. Now only 53 yards or so of soil being removed and 495 gallons of water is not much. So there still is an environmental issue. ● If you go and put new infrastructure in the ground (i.e. sewers, water lines or whatever) you are introducing a conduit for migration unless somebody undertakes thorough cleanup of existing contaminates. ● The other issue is the well head protection act. 800 feet is the setback and there are at least 5 wells within 800 feet. So, installing new tanks will require special permitting and authorization through both LARA, EGLE and the local health department. ● The tanks in the ground right now are out of compliance. ● The owner/operator took the property on as is, which is fine, but give him obligations under LARA. ● The last time I checked 3 years ago the tanks were not capped. John Adams and Leslie Deboer (BLDI 931 Interchange Dr. Holland, MI 49423) ● Agreed with LARA and EGLE details discussed by others ● Disagrees with the majority of what was said. ● With regards to wells, distances, depth and what the soils are at the location, we have approval from LARA and DEQ for tank replacement. ● The State looks at these sites as a positive thing, of getting old tanks out of the ground. The tanks that are there are steel tanks that will decay over time. The only way to clean the site out is to properly remove them. Have an environmental company come in and they will dictate soils that need to come out. So, pretty much this site has been approved by LARA and DEQ for replacement. 10-5-2026 PC Minutes ● With respect to the wells and setback distance, ultimately with sites like this LARA will not approve them to go in within those distances unless full evaluation has been done to show that the geology there is going to be protective of those wells. So, even the Township issuing a special land use permit for a gas station to go in there, that does not mean that you are approving the tanks to go into the ground in any way shape or form. They still have to go through the proper channels. And LARA certainly will not let tanks go in the ground unless all that has been looked at. This is the very first thing that we will look at on any project. We are part of the members of Michigan Petroleum Association. So, I will immediately do my evaluation and send it to LARA for review. And basically, if LARA says hey, we need to stop, so no one has to spend money. On some would say on well reference Leslie would be the person I would contact, based on clay depth, based on sand, gravel and water movement. Is this worth going for a variance, because it is extremely expensive. In this case it was approved without any variance. Sites that have tanks, you know that well distances don’t matter if it’s a one-toone replacement. This particular location, when I looked at the well map, was very easy. It's a website that you can measure distances, they would be fine to put tanks in, anywhere on the site, not just in that location. ● Anytime you replace tanks or 50% piping you have to have an environmental company involved. They are the ones that will dig samples and they are the ones that will dictate what we can do as a contractor. ● The geology on this site, while it might be true that there could be limited water that could be shallow. The deeper aquifers the ones that these wells are screened within. All the wells in the area are bedrock wells. That’s overlayed by about 60 – 80 feet minimum of clay so it is very, very protective of the drinking water wells. He does have obligations as the owner of the property. ● You cannot evaluate vapor intrusions while the building systems HVAC are running. So, there are a lot of elements that go into that stuff that would be determined and decided based on the use, based on the redevelopment. He has tank plans; he’s not putting in steel tanks. Those are all the important things to know. You have a vacant building just sitting there with tanks in the ground. He is not saying he is going to reopen the station with those same tanks. 10-5-2026 PC Minutes ● He will be replacing those tanks and the tanks that are red tagged currently you do not have to do any testing or anything on red tagged tanks. Basically, they were CP protected tank tags where you want them to come out of the ground. The sooner they come out of the ground the better. And tanks and everything put in today; anything post 2008 have to have double walls and piping annual tank and line testing every 3 years you have to test containment sumps. Anything prior to 2008 none of that was required. ● This site would be setting a new standard and spending a lot of money and testing to make sure quarterly inspections are done. ● He has an environmental company that is working alongside him and a reputable oil company. He is doing all the right things. Right now, there is an eyesore on the corner. You have somebody that wants to take and redevelop it. Increase the aesthetics of the area, make it actually useable and create jobs and things like that. And again, he is going through all the right channels before anything can be done. David McDade – (Roark Galt Architects) ● A couple of things that were brought up. One was traffic concerns; we are going to start the process with Genesee County Road Commission. Which I had a conversation with them about that today. ● They wanted us to get a traffic count as well. ● We didn’t want to start some of this before receiving a special use permit. Because all of that final approval has to be done within site plan. We completely understand and we are heading that direction. ● Concerns about non aesthetics is not an issue. I feel what we are doing on that corner will make it a wow factor. Property owner wants the building to look good. I personally am most proud of this one. Kim Carlson (Surveyor)● Storm water on site. Retention requirements or needs. ● Disturbed area is less than an acre ● Less than half an acre does not require detention of stormwater 10-5-2026 PC Minutes Chris Czyzio – ● The other gas station owned by Mr. Hansen the same issues came up. ● I don’t remember the exact number of water wells in the area. However we did work with the State of Michigan and it was determined that all those wells were well outside the range. ● As everything else, Mr. Hansen had to fulfill all of the requirements as well. A traffic study has been provided that was conducted by Fleis & VandenBrink on behalf of the petitioner for future conditions and site circulation. The study had the following conclusions: a. Future conditions of the site are expected to account for less than 5% of total traffic volume along study roadways and any impact from the site is expected to be negligible. b. The projected drive-through evaluation indicates that during peak operations, the max anticipated stacking spaces of 3 past the payment kiosk is expected to adequately accommodate the site, without exceeding the internal site circulation and impacting the adjacent roadway network. 4. MDOT has provided the following comment that should be addressed in regard to the traffic study: Traffic counts were collected during several significant ramp closures in this area. The I-96 westbound on-ramp at Latson Road was closed during the counts, as were the two Grand River Avenue on/off ramps at I-96. As a result, traffic movements were affected by these closures (even though the overall traffic volumes were generally comparable. For example, the PM peak-hour volume for westbound Grand River Avenue was approximately 1,967 vehicles per hour in 2025, compared with only 1,498 vehicles in 2026 a 23% decrease. Given these significant volume variations, the TIS does not provide a fair representation of typical traffic conditions. Furthermore, despite the substantial differences in existing turning movement volumes, the TIS indicates that at least one movement at Latson Road and Grand River Avenue is projected to deteriorate from Level of Service (LOS) E to LOS F in the PM peak. This would not be acceptable under MDOT standards. Mr. Reiber is concerned with the increase in traffic. Although it is only a five percent increase, it is still an increase. He asked why the drive thru lane is on the south side of the building and visible from Grand River. She noted there is another proposed outlot project in the Hobby Lobby parking lot that will not be able to move forward until the connection is in place. Mr. Hadjinian agrees that the connection will help with the traffic on Grand River and will benefit the patrons and businesses of both of these sites. 3 Genoa Charter Township Planning Commission Meeting September 14, 2026 Approved Minutes Chairperson McCreary read an email received today from MDOT regarding the traffic study. Ms. Kroll explained how the traffic study was performed. She has spoken to Mr. Fournier from MDOT and they agree that the intersection of Latson & Grand River is at capacity, there is no way to make improvements, and the cross connection is a benefit. She stated that outlots in a Meijer parking lot are complimentary uses. Drivers go from Meijer to the outlot or vice versa so separate use. Chairperson McCreary does not agree with a traffic study that was done during the I-96 construction. Mr. Chouinard agrees. Mr. Reiber stated there is no data to show that the cross access easement will assist with the traffic. Mr. Weisberger noted that the applicant will be paying for the completion of the cross access drive; Meijer is not going to do it. Mr. Andre explained how they will address the light spill-over The Brighton Area Fire Authority Fire Marshals letter dated August 28, 2026 states all previous comments have been resolved by the applicant on the most recent submittal. The Fire Authority has no further comments on the project unless additional revisions are made. Chairperson McCreary reviewed a letter received from a resident in opposition to the project. Mr. Reiber reviewed all the deviations that are being requested in the amended PUD. There were reasons why these were in the original agreement. He is not comfortable with this. Mr. Chouinard stated the deviations are caused by the building being built into an existing parking lot. Mr. Chouinard stated that the cross access drive should help with the traffic but agrees that there is no data. Also, MDOT said that the traffic increase is not acceptable. Ms. Kroll reviewed details of her traffic study, noting that this development will increase the traffic by 22 cars in the morning and 66 in the afternoon. She noted that the entire intersection is not rated an F, it is only the northbound traffic straight through the intersection. The entire intersection is rated D, which is acceptable in southeast Michigan. The increase of less than five percent at this intersection is negligible and would not be noticed. Mr. Borden stated only three of the deviations listed in the PUD Agreement are actual deviations. Four of them are able to be waived by the Planning Commission. The call to the public was made at 8:47 pm. Mr. Matt Hurley of 4070 Brookstone Court stated that during the recent master plan activity, it was noted that there are many unused commercial properties in the area, so why do new buildings need to be built. A. Summary 1. Amended PUD Agreement: a. The revised draft Agreement includes a requirement to construct a cross-access connection with the development to the west. b. 4 of the 9 dimensional deviations noted are allowed with Planning Commission approval (reduced parking setbacks, buffer zone width, and spacing between drive-through uses). c. The applicant must address any comments provided by Township staff and/or the Township Attorney on the draft PUD Agreement. 2. PUD Conceptual Plan: a. The proposal generally meets the Conceptual PUD Plan standards of Section 10.07.01, provided that the Commission finds that this amendment does not alter the previously established PUD qualification standards or the public benefit demonstrated for this site. b. The proposal generally meets the MUPUD standards of Section 10.03.03. c. The Commission should consider comments provided by the Township Engineer and/or Brighton Area Fire Authority. 3. Site Plan Comments: a. Details for the outdoor eating area will need to be provided on the Final PUD Plan. b. Details of the cross-access between Meijer and the commercial center to the west will need to be depicted on the Final PUD Plan. c. Minor corrections are needed to the Impact Assessment with respect to the inclusion of a drivethrough restaurant and the impervious surface ratio. B. Proposal/Process/Background The applicant proposes to create a new 1.68-acre outlot in the southeast corner of the existing Meijer property; an area currently occupied by parking that is seldom used. The proposed outlot is intended for development of a multi-tenant commercial building, including a restaurant with a drive-through (5,620 square feet of gross floor area). Since no outlot was contemplated for this area of the PUD and a drive-through restaurant is not currently an allowable use in this PUD, the applicant has applied to amend the approved PUD. In accordance with Section 10.11, the proposal has been deemed a major amendment to the PUD. As such, the Planning Commission is to review and put forth recommendations to the Township Board on the Conceptual PUD Plan, Impact Assessment, and amended PUD Agreement. www.safebuilt.com Genoa Township Planning Commission Howell Outlot 1, LLC Amendment to an Approved PUD (Review #3) Page 3 It is important to note that of the 9 deviations noted, 4 of them are allowed with Planning Commission discretion. More specifically, the parking setbacks (items A and B), buffer zone width (item C), and spacing between drive-through uses (item E) are allowed with Commission approval. Additionally, the applicant must address any comments provided by Township staff and/or the Township Attorney. D. PUD Conceptual Plan 1. Submittal Requirements. The revised submittal includes the information required by Ordinance. 2. Conceptual PUD Plan Standards. We provide the following comments with respect to the standards of Section 10.07.01: As an established PUD, the qualification requirements have previously been deemed to be met for this site and public benefit demonstrated however, the Commission should find that this amendment does not alter the previously established PUD qualification standards or the public benefit demonstrated for this site. The proposed amendment is generally consistent with the Master Plan classification of West Grand River – Mixed Use, which is “envisioned for a higher intensity of commercial and residential uses than the East Grand River District.” This location within the PUD does not appear to contain any significant or historic features that need to be protected. Given the location and nature of surrounding uses, we believe necessary infrastructure is already in place; however, the Commission should consider any comments provided by the Township Engineer. There is an existing bike path along Latson Road that provides non-motorized access/connections throughout this part of the Township. The project includes an outdoor seating area, which is not necessarily a common open space area, but generally meets the intent of such (in our opinion). Dimensional deviations are identified in the draft amendment to the PUD Agreement. 3. MUPUD Standards. We provide the following comments with respect to the standards of Section 10.03.03: The inclusion of fast casual restaurants and one with a drive-through is generally compatible with the land use pattern in this area of the Township. As previously noted, this PUD does not currently permit a restaurant with a drive-through; hence the request for amendment. The Ordinance contains use requirements for restaurants with drive-throughs (Section 7.02.02j) and outdoor seating (Section 7.02.02i), both of which will need to be me as part of the Final PUD Plan submittal (if the amendment is approved). Based on the calculations provided on Sheet C3.1, the proposed Outlot will provide 45.7% pervious surface, which exceeds the 25% minimum open space requirement. As previously noted, there is an existing bike path along Latson Road that provides linkages to other sites/amenities in this area of the Township. As a site that currently contains a parking lot, we do not foresee an issue with the amount of usable upland area as part of the open space. The proposed Outlot exceeds minimum GCD standards for lot area and width. As previously noted, the project includes 5 dimensional deviations (building setback, no short-term waiting or dedicated RV spaces, a parking reduction for Meijer, and minor light spill-over) and use of Planning Commission discretion for 4 other items (parking setbacks, buffer zone width, and spacing between drive-through uses). HOWELL TOWNSHIP REGULAR BOARD MEETING MINUTES 3525 Byron Rd. Howell, MI 48855 October 13, 2026 6:30 P.M. MEMBERS PRESENT: Robert Spaulding Sue Daus Jonathan Hohenstein Matthew Counts Tim Boal Jodi Fulton Bob Wilson MEMBERS ABSENT: Supervisor Clerk Treasurer Trustee Trustee Trustee Trustee Also in Attendance: 12 people signed in Phil Westmoreland with Spicer Group, Jason Lipa with Schafer Construction, Lynn Whipple with PEA Group, Brad Klein with AKA Architects and Kristofer Enlow with Beckett & Raeder. Supervisor Spaulding called the meeting to order at 6:30 p.m. The roll was called. Supervisor Spaulding requested members rise for the Pledge of Allegiance. CALL TO THE BOARD: Trustee Boal requested to add agenda item 8-H, NDA discussion. APPROVAL OF THE AGENDA: Motion by Boal, Second by Fulton, “To accept the agenda with the addition.” Motion carried. 2 dissents. APPROVAL OF BOARD MEETING MINUTES: September 14, 2026 REGULAR BOARD MEETING MINUTES Treasurer Hohenstein requested a correction to Treasurer's report in the previous minutes, changing “Marie” to “Marnie.” Motion by Hohenstein, Second by Daus, “To accept the minutes as amended.” Motion carried. CALL TO THE PUBLIC: Angela Barbash read a letter on behalf of Kristin Dennison: In opposition to the proposed DTE Natural Gas Plan for Handy Township. Angela Barbash, 4211 Crandall Rd.: Spoke on NDAs. Bob Wilson, 2945 Brewer Rd.: Spoke on attorney fee appropriations, office equipment, American Legion and Fagan violation. 1 10-13-2026 UNFINISHED BUSINESS: A. Master Plan Update – Discussion The Board discussed the timing and budget considerations for the proposed Master Plan update. Concerns were raised regarding planning workload and project timelines. B. Engine Brake Ordinance – Discussion The Board discussed options for engine braking concerns within the township. It was the consensus of the Board for Clerk Daus to contact Marion Township regarding their sign installation process and enforceability, as well as contact the Livingston County Road Commission to review installation parameters and approval requirements for the installation of a sign. NEW BUSINESS: A. Data Center Moratorium Extension Motion by Wilson, Second by Hohenstein, “To accept the Data Center Moratorium Ordinance No. 299.” Board discussion regarding the procedures for extending the data center moratorium, with the Board emphasizing the critical priority of completing and adopting the data center ordinance. Roll call vote: Wilson – yes, Counts – yes, Boal – yes, Daus – yes, Fulton – yes, Hohenstein – yes, Spaulding – yes. Motion carried (7-0). B. Wage and Benefit Study The Board discussed initiating a Wage and Benefit Study to evaluate employee compensation and benefit structures relative to comparable municipalities. Motion by Counts, Second by Daus, “To accept a proposal to conduct classification and compensation study from Municipal Consulting Services as presented.” Board discussion followed. Motion carried. C. Financial Report – First Quarter Deputy Supervisor Kilpela presented an overview of the Township’s first-quarter financial report for the period ending September 30, 2026. The presentation covered the Township’s overall financial position—including the General, Road, and Sewer & Water funds, as well as current legal fees. Deputy Supervisor Kilpela responded to questions from the Board. D. Land Division Ordinance Deputy Supervisor Kilpela presented a draft of the general land division ordinance prepared in response to upcoming state statutory changes that will become effective March 2027. By consensus, the Board agreed to submit the draft to the Township Attorney for legal review prior to bringing it back for potential adoption at a future meeting. E. PC2026-11 Nabil Bazzi, Request to rezone Parcel #4706-21-300-028, Vacant Land from Industrial Flex (IFZ) to Neighborhood Service Commercial (NSC) The Board discussed the potential rezoning from Industrial Flex Zone (IFZ) to Neighborhood Service Commercial (NSC). The Board reviewed recommendations from the Planning Commission, Township Planner, and the County Planning Commission. Discussion followed regarding Master Plan alignment, permitted NSC uses, lot size, and the zoning of the surrounding area. Motion by Boal, Second by Wilson, “To approve rezoning of parcel 4706-21-300-028 PC2026-11 from IFZ to NSC with the following findings. Although the rezoning classification does not align with the defined uses of the master plans in this particular parcel, the proposed uses under NSC are similar and complementary to the neighboring parcels in the current zoning. Also, the location and size of the parcel allows the rezoning to be compatible to the surrounding area uses and equally or better suited than the current zoning with no significant impact to public 2 10-13-2026 services or facilities likely beyond the current zoning.” Discussion followed. Roll call vote: Fulton – yes, Boal – yes, Wilson – yes, Counts – yes, Hohenstein – no, Spaulding – yes, Daus – yes. Motion carried. (6-1) F. Proposed 2027 Fee Schedule Treasurer Hohenstein presented the proposed 2027 fee schedule. Board discussion followed. It was the consensus of the Board to revise the zoning fee structure and bring the updated proposed fee schedule back to a future meeting for Board consideration. G. Tooley Road Park Proposals A total of seven (7) proposals were received for services to develop the site plan for the Tooley Road Park. Following interviews and evaluation, PEA Group and Beckett & Raeder received the highest overall scores. Discussion followed regarding the selection process and whether to proceed with one or both firms for contract negotiations to move the project forward. Phil Westmoreland from Spicer Group answered questions from the Board. Lynn Whipple with PEA Group and Brad Klein with AKA Architects introduced themselves and answered questions from the Board. Kristofer Enlow with Beckett & Raeder introduced himself. Board discussion followed. Motion by Fulton, Second by Hohenstein, “To put forward both contract negotiations for PEA Group and Beckett & Raeder at the same time for the Park Project for Tooley.” Motion carried. Board discussion followed regarding the selection process for construction management services, including whether to conduct a competitive selection process. Motion by Hohenstein, Second by Daus, “To enter into contract negotiations with Schafer Construction for the construction management portion of the project.” Board discussion followed. Jason Lipa with Schafer Construction answered questions from the Board. Roll call vote: Daus – yes, Hohenstein – yes, Spaulding – no, Counts – no, Boal – no, Fulton – no, Wilson – no. Motion failed. (2-5) H. NDA – Discussion The Board discussed whether to address Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) through a standalone policy or an ordinance. Board members reviewed sample language from other townships and considered legal enforcement and associated costs. Board consensus was to prepare a draft standalone NDA policy for review by the Township Attorney, with further discussion regarding the policy versus ordinance approach to occur at a future meeting. CALL TO THE PUBLIC: Angela Barbash, 4211 Crandall Rd.: Spoke in opposition to the proposed gas plant near the Township border. REPORTS: A. SUPERVISOR: Supervisor Spaulding reported speaking with Todd Musson of the Livingston County Road Commission, who recommended scheduling a meeting to discuss township road matters. B. TREASURER: See report C. CLERK: No report 3 10-13-2026 D. ZONING: Zoning Administrator Hohenstein reported identifying non-compliant uses through state verification requests asking the Township to confirm compliance with local zoning ordinances. The Board reached a consensus to address violations identified during these reviews and work collaboratively with property owners to bring the uses into compliance. E. ASSESSING: See report F. FIRE AUTHORITY: Supervisor Spaulding reported on recent purchases, noting that new gear and helmets were acquired to replace outdated equipment to ensure firefighter safety. Additionally, a new riding lawn mower was purchased for the fire station located at Chase Lake and Oak Grove Roads. G. MHOG: Trustee Counts reported that approximately 89 million gallons of water were produced in August and noted that the cross-country main is near completion, with Section B now operational. Additionally, severe weather and widespread power outages across pump stations in early September required substantial staff overtime. Portable generators were deployed to maintain water and wastewater services and prevent basement sewage backups. In response to these events, MHOG is implementing a State of Emergency Policy to establish protocols for staff compensation during emergency operations. H. PLANNING COMMISSION: Trustee Boal reported on the preliminary site plan review for a proposed landscaping business on Mason Road, reviewed a temporary use permit on Burkhart Road, and continued discussions on the High-Impact Land Use Ordinance. I. ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS (ZBA): No Report J. WWTP: Treasurer Hohenstein reported Board approval is needed for a sewer main repair. Motion by Hohenstein, Second by Daus, “To approve the estimate from D’Angelo Brothers to replace the broken main as presented.” Motion carried. Treasurer Hohenstein presented the MHOG budget for Board consideration. Motion by Counts, Second by Hohenstein, “To approve the MHOG budget as presented.” Motion carried. K. HAPRA: No report L. PROPERTY COMMITTEE: No report M. PARK & RECREATION COMMITTEE: No report 4 10-13-2026 N. SHIAWASSEE RIVER COMMITTEE: Supervisor Spaulding reported plans to coordinate a meeting with Treasurer Hohenstein, Trustee Wilson, Deputy Supervisor Kilpela, and Ken Recker of the Livingston County Drain Commissioner's Office to discuss project options and township funding considerations regarding the Shiawassee River. Supervisor Spaulding will report his findings back to the Board following the discussion. O. TRUSTEE: Trustee Wilson reported that the pothole issue on Brewer Road has been resolved. Trustee Boal expressed appreciation to all the volunteers who assisted with the Township Fall Cleanup Day. Trustee Fulton discussed concerns regarding the proposed natural gas power plant and requested that the topic be placed on the upcoming agenda for further discussion. DISBURSEMENTS: REGULAR PAYMENTS AND CHECK REGISTER: Motion by Hohenstein, Second by Daus, “To accept the disbursements as presented and any normal and customary payments for the month.” Motion carried. ADJOURNMENT: Motion by Counts, Second by Hohenstein, “To adjourn” Motion carried. The meeting was adjourned at 9:57 p.m. ___ Robert Spaulding, Howell Township Supervisor ___ Sue Daus, Howell Township Clerk ___ Tanya Davidson, Recording Secretary 5 10-13-2026 A.B. The Township Supervisor is the moderator of the meeting. In the absence of the Supervisor, the Township Clerk shall hold an election of the Board Members present to select a moderator for the meeting. Anyone attending the meeting either in-person or on-line may speak during the “Call to the Public” part of the meeting. To preserve order, those attending in- person will speak first. When all in-person attendees have been heard, the moderator will ask if any on-line attendee wishes to speak. When recognized by the moderator, in-person attendees shall come to the podium. The moderator will request that they give their name and address before they begin their comments. When all in-person attendees have finished speaking, the moderator will ask if anyone attending the meeting on-line wishes to speak. On-line attendees may unmute themselves and when recognized by the moderator may speak. On-line attendees will also be asked for their name and address. All comments shall be addressed to the Township Board. The “Call to the Public” is for attendees to provide information or opinions to the Township Board and is not intended to be a dialog. Anyone needing a response should contact officials or staff during working hours. To preserve efficiency, speakers will be asked to keep their comments to three minutes or less. On some occasions, attendees may be asked for comments during agenda items. ADOPTED ON 08/25/2022; AMENDED ON 02/12/2026

text: TOWNSHIP BOARD MEETING TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 10, 2026 Welcome to the Napoleon Township Board Meeting. We appreciate your attendance. Board Members receive their packets in advance, allowing an opportunity to prepare for the meeting and be ready to conduct the business of the Township efficiently. Our meetings usually finish in less than an hour. Before the meeting starts, please turn off or mute all electronic devices. Our meeting will proceed according to the agenda that follows. The first public comment is limited to items on the agenda and is for a maximum of 2 minutes per person and 10 minutes per subject. After a non-routine motion is made by the Board, seconded, and discussed, the Supervisor may ask for public comment before the formal vote of the Board is taken. Comments are limited to 2 minutes per person. The last public comment is open for any Township business to be addressed and is limited to 2 minutes per person. For all public comment, please stand and state your full name and residence address. All comments are directed to the Township Board. Thank you for your interest in Napoleon Township. We hope to see you at future meetings. Please Note: During public comment the Board does not answer questions and does not engage in discussion or debate with the person making the comment. DAN WYMER SUPERVISOR TRACI SPRING CLERK ANITA GRAHAM TREASURER JOHN HUMMER TRUSTEE JULIE STAGE TRUSTEE NAPOLEON TOWNSHIP TOWNSHIP HALL 6755 Brooklyn Rd Napoleon, MI www.napoleontownship.us CALL TO ORDER 6:00 PM - TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 10, 2026 PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE APPROVAL OF AGENDA e Motion to Accept or Motion to Change CONSENT AGENDA e Approval of Minutes — October 13 Regular Board Meeting October 13 Lakeview Special Assessment Public Hearing 2 October 13 Wolf Lake Canal Special Assessment Public Hearing 1 e Payment of Claims PUBLIC COMMENT - Agenda Items Only COMMUNITY SERVICE RECOGNITION —- OCT 17 CLEANUP DAY e Josh’s Dumpsters - Joshua Blakeman e Napoleon High School Students COUNTY COMMISSION REPORT —- Commissioner Kennedy DEPARTMENT MONTHLY REPORTS Fire Police Ordinance Enforcement Building & Zoning Assessing Sewer & Water Operations Planning Commission Zoning Board of Appeals NEW BUSINESS Employee Holiday Bonuses Police and Fire Chief Retention Bonuses (Per Employment Contracts) Industrial Rehabilitation District Aggies 3 Year Event Permit Renewal Payroll Processing UNFINISHED BUSINESS e Wolf Lake Canal Weed Special Assessment — Resolution Confirming Special Assessment Roll e Unpaid Bills Grace Period (Before Going On Property Tax) UPDATES e Election e Blood Drive December 28 e Crypt Roof Project e EGLE Intent to Apply Filing PUBLIC COMMENT- Any Township Business Adjourn Minutes of Napoleon Township Regular Board Meeting - DRAFT October 13, 2026 Call to Order at 6:00 p.m. by Supervisor Wymer with members Graham, Hummer, Spring and Stage. Pledge of Allegiance APPROVAL OF AGENDA AND CONSENT AGENDA: Motion by Graham, support by Stage to approve the agenda including the consent agenda, with the payment of claims GOF = $85,662.54 and Restricted = $91,860.05, minutes of the September 8 Lakeview Special Assessment Public Hearing 1, and minutes of the September 8, 2026 regular board meeting as amended. Motion passed. PUBLIC COMMENT - AGENDA ITEMS ONLY: Robert Farrell of 5629 S. Meridian Road spoke regarding garbage being dumped on Hart Road. Thomas Wilson of 3981 Miles Road spoke regarding data centers. Bonnie Gretzner of 7789 Napoleon Road spoke regarding data centers. Sally Haupt of 8855 Bellemere Ct. asked why data centers was on the agenda. COUNTY COMMISSIONER REPORT: Commissioner Kennedy provided updates from the Jackson County Department of Transportation. DEPARTMENT MONTHLY REPORTS: Fire: Chief Bickford’s said there 62 calls for service in September, 12 of which were in Norvell Township for a total of 652 calls year-to-date. \ Police: Deputy Chief Peters reported 280 Central Dispatch calls for service and a total of 277 other investigations in September. He reported good participation from the five officers on the reserve corp. Wellsby, one of the reserve officers, is working Tom Freeman at the school. Staffing and scheduling is a challenge. Ordinance Enforcement: Jeff Kirkpatrick reported normal activity. Assessing, Zoning, & Building: Written report for Building provided by Jane Gallant. Written report for Assessing provided by Lisa from All Level Assessing. Sewer & Water Operations: Wymer said a new pump was installed at the lift station at the corner of Wolf Lake Road and Mack Island Road. The previous pump was hit by lightning and the lift has been operating on a portable pump since then. Wymer is working with a consulting service at no charge to search for a solution to the township’s water system freeze including applying for grants. Planning Commission: Hummer reported the commission did not meet in September and will meet on October 22 at 6 PM for a case. Page 1 of 4 October 13, 2026 Napoleon Township -DRAFT Minutes of Regular Board Meeting Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA): Stage reported the ZBA is meeting October 14" for two cases. One is on South Portage for a garage addition and the second on Sandbeach Road for a cover over a deck. NEW BUSINESS: Bucket Brigade Contribution for Halloween Event: Motion by Stage to approve spending $400 towards the purchase of candy for the annual Halloween Event on October 31 at the fire station, support by Wymer. Roll Call: Wymer — AYE, Graham — AYE, Hummer — AYE, Stage- AYE, Spring - AYE. Motion carried. Cooling Unit Replacement in Electrical Equipment Room: Three quotes were presented for consideration to replace the cooling unit in the electrical equipment room. Motion by Hummer to accept the bid from Paul Bengel to remove the bad cooling unit and install a new mini- split unit in the amount of $4,950, support by Graham. Roll Call: Graham —- AYE, Hummer — AYE, Stage- AYE, Spring - AYE, Wymer — AYE. Motion carried. Quarterly Budget Adjustment: Motion by Wymer to approve Resolution Number 1 to Adjust the 2026-2027 General Operating Fund Budget as presented, support by Stage. Roll Call: Hummer — AYE, Stage- AYE, Spring - AYE, Wymer — AYE, Graham — AYE. Motion carried. Josh’s Dumpster — Offer of Cleanup Events: Wymer said Josh from Josh’s Dumpster contacted him to offer to bring dumpsters to the township for local residents. Wymer thanked him and suggested they come on the October 17 when tires will collected at the township. Data Center Discussion: Hummer suggested the township should be prepared in case we get an application for a data center in Napoleon Township. He shared a two-page document that defined what a data center is and does along with pros and cons. He said two other area townships have adopted a temporary moratorium opposing data centers. Wymer suggested we look at what other townships are doing and what guardrails they’ ve put in place to determine what we may want to add or change in our ordinances. Stage did some research and said townships should review their current zoning ordinances and act before a company buys property or submits an application. She suggested a committee be formed and offered to form a committee. Hummer indicated he was interested in being on the committee. Hummer wondered whether this should be a planning commission item? It was suggested this topic be brought up at the next planning commission meeting for discussion then bring a recommendation to the board. UNFINISHED BUSINESS: Commuter Parking Area Marking ty TRI-County Striping: Wymer thanked TRI-County Striping for painting the new 9 commuter spots at no charge. Commuter Parking Area Rules & Signage: Wymer shared proposed new rules for the new commuter parking area. Motion by Wymer to accept the rules as presented and have signage created, support by Graham. Page 2 of 4 October 13, 2026 Napoleon Township -DRAFT Minutes of Regular Board Meeting Roll Call: Hummer — AYE, Stage- AYE, Spring - AYE, Wymer — AYE, Graham — AYE. Motion carried. Wolf Lake Canal Weed Special Assessment District — Resolution Continuing the Process First public hearing was held October 13 at 5:30 PM. There were no objections to the project or the parcels listed. Second public hearing is scheduled for Tuesday, November 10, 2026 at 5:00PM. Motion by Wymer to approve the Resolution Continuing Process to Establish Wolf Lake Canal Special Assessment District, support by Hummer. Roll Call: Stage- AYE, Spring - AYE, Wymer— AYE, Graham — AYE, Hummer — AYE. Motion carried. Lakeview Avenue Road Special Assessment District — Resolution Confirming Special Assessment Roll First public hearing was held September 8 at SPM. There were no objections to the project or the parcels listed. Second public hearing was held Tuesday, October 13, 2026 at 5:00PM. There were no objections to the parcels listed. Motion by Wymer to approve the Resolution Confirming Special Assessment Roll of Lakeview Drive Special Assessment for Road Improvements, support by Stage. Roll Call: Spring - AYE, Wymer — AYE, Graham — AYE, Hummer — AYE, Stage- AYE. Motion carried. Crypt Roof Replacement & Grant from Napoleon Benefit Fund Spring said Ryan Watts and Craig Pittman have secured donations to fifl the $4,000 gap. Motion by Wymer to approve Clerk Spring signing a contract with Property Restoration for replacement and repair of the Cemetery Crypt Roof, support by Hummer. Motion carried. Trail Cameras to Catch Dumpsters: Motion by Wymer to authorize Deputy Chief Peters to spend up to $1,200 for the purchase of new cameras to catch illegal dumpers. Funding will come from the General Operating Fund under Projects, support by Hummer. Roll Call: Graham — AYE, Hummer — AYE, Stage- AYE, Spring - AYE, Wymer —- AYE. Motion carried. UPDATES: Upcoming Election: Spring reported that over 1,300 absentee ballots were mailed October 1. Early voting runs from October 24 — November 1 at Grass Lake Charter Township. Voting on Tuesday, November 3 will be at the township. The township received a reimbursement of $2,700 spent on wages for early voting workers. Tire Collection Event Wymer updated the board about the event on Saturday, October 17" which also includes Josh’s Dumpsters being on site to allow residents to get rid of other items at no cost. Page 3 of 4 October 13, 2026 Napoleon Township -DRAFT Minutes of Regular Board Meeting Unemployment Benefits Hearing Outcome: Wymer said the administrative law judge ruled in the township’s favor, but the former employee has filed for an appeal. Safety Concerns — Floor Mats Replaced: Due to a fall on a floor mat earlier this year, Wymer approved the selection of a different floor mat provider. There was no penalty to cancel the service with the current floor mat provider. County Gravel Processing Resumes at Blue Ridge Pit: Wymer said the Jackson County Department of Transportation intends to resume processing gravel on Blue Ridge Road which could eventually eliminate the large hill on Blue Ridge Road. PUBLIC COMMENT - Any Township Business Craig Pittman of 40 Ackerson Lake Road asked about township ordinances regarding signs and homeless encampments. Thomas Wilson of 3981 Miles Road spoke regarding quickly putting in a short-term moratorium against data centers. Christine Mackenzie spoke regarding a large property going up for auction soon and questioned whether a data center company might purchase it. Ruth Crandall commented on the condition of Cook and Blue Ridge Roads. Bonnie Gretzner of 7789 Napoleon Road spoke regarding data centers. Julie Stage thanked Ryan Watts for the history that he is sharing about the area. She also thanked Craig Pittman for work he does to clean headstones which was applauded by those present. Adjourn: 7:13 PM Traci Spring, Clerk Dan Wymer, Supervisor Page 4 of 4 October 13, 2026 Napoleon Township -DRAFT Minutes of Regular Board Meeting

All Districts: The use of Temporary Portable Storage containers in prohibited in all districts with the following exceptions: a. Up to 10 Temporary Portable Storage Containers are allowed on premises in the 11 (Light Industrial) zoning district. Containers may not be stacked or in any required setback area. b. Up to 20 Temporary Portable Storage Containers are allowed on premises in the I2 (General Industrial) zoning district. Containers may not be stacked or in any required setback area. C. One (1) Temporary Portable Storage Container is allowed in a residential zoning district for up to 30 days as part of a professional moving service for relocation purposes or operations; provided a permit has been obtained from the Zoning Administrator or their designee. Temporary Portable Storage Containers used for construction purposes must be approved by the Richfield Township Zoning Administrator prior to placement when used during construction for up to tessthan twelve (12) months. The Zoning Administrator Planning Commission has the authority to authorize but is not required to approve the use of Temporary Portable Storage Containers for construction or remodel purposes for any period in excess of twelve months. A Temporary Portable Storage Container may not be used as a dwelling or living quarters, nor for camping, cooking or recreation purposes for any amount of time in any district. Any Temporary Portable Storage Container existing on any property in the Township of Richfield on the date of final passage of this ordinance shall either be removed from such property or be brought into compliance with the provisions of this section within thirty (30) days of final passage of this ordinance. 227 RICHFIELD TOWNSHIP ORDINANCE NO. An ordinance to amend Article XIX of the Township Zoning Ordinance by adding a new section 1903 regarding moratoriums. THE TOWNSHIP OF RICHFIELD ORDAINS: Section 1. Amendment of Article XIX of the Township Zoning Ordinance. The Township Board hereby amends Article XIX of the Township Zoning Ordinance by adding thereto a new Section 1903, entitled “Moratoriums,” to read as follows: SECTION 1903 MORATORIUMS 1. Moratorium by Resolution. The Township Board, by resolution, may impose a temporary moratorium upon the review or issuance of any and all applications, permits, rezonings, licenses, or approvals for specific special or other new or emerging land uses in the Township if the Township Board desires to review, enact, or amend provisions of the master plan or zoning ordinance to regulate specific special or other new or emerging land uses that may impact the health, safety or welfare of Township residents or property. 2. Purpose and Findings. The resolution must state the purpose of the moratorium and include findings of the Township Board in support of the moratorium. 3. Length of Moratorium Any resolution adopted pursuant to this section must specify the length of the moratorium, which may not exceed twelve (12) months. The resolution may provide for one (1) extension of the moratorium, by resolution, for up to six (6) months. 3. Notice. Notice of the resolution must be published within seven (7) days of its adoption. The notice must include the following: (a) | Asummary of the resolution's effect. (b) | The length of the moratorium and whether an extension is possible. (c) Where the public may inspect the resolution enacting the moratorium. Section 2. Effective Date. This Ordinance shall take effect 30 days following publication. As part of this effort, they incorporated adopted amendments, corrected formatting and numbering inconsistencies, updated section references, and addressed other non-substantive errors (Please review their memo for additional details). The e-mail with the links to attachments shared by CW has been forwarded to the PC. ON-GOING REVIEW We are currently making additional formatting and organizational improvements to enhance readability, accessibility, and online navigation. The revised document will be available online by Nov 09. These changes are intended to improve the ordinance's usability in both digital and printed formats without altering the substance of the regulations. These revisions include: 1. Section Headers: Adding color to section headings to improve visual organization and distinguish sections. 2. Consistent Numbering: Standardizing the numbering and formatting hierarchy throughout the ordinance: Heading 1 Article Heading 2 Section Heading 3 A. Heading 4 Heading 5 3. 1. a. Heading 6 i. Tables: Numbering items within tables to make ordinance provisions easier to reference and cite. 4. Illustrations: Moving illustrations closer to the corresponding text to minimize back-and-forth navigation. 5. Page Layout: Ensuring each article begins on a right-hand (odd-numbered) page for double-sided printing. 6. Cross-References: Reviewing and correcting section references throughout the document. 7. Hyperlinks: Underlining clickable text so links are easily identifiable. 8. Navigation: Adding a link to the Table of Contents on every page for convenient navigation. Page 8 of 26 NEXT STEPS Due to incomplete historical adoption records, the previous consultant recommended repealing and readopting the consolidated Zoning Ordinance in its entirety, following review by the Township Attorney. We agree with this recommendation and propose the following steps: 1. November Planning Commission Meeting The purpose of the November meeting is to introduce the consolidated Zoning Ordinance, summarize the work completed by the previous consultant and the additional improvements underway, and explain the proposed review and readoption process. No formal action is requested at this meeting. 2. Planning Commission Review A draft of the consolidated ordinance is available on the Township website. Given the length of the document, Planning Commission members are encouraged to focus on sections they are familiar with and identify: • Missing Information: Regulations or amendments that may have been omitted. • Inconsistencies: Conflicts between use tables, definitions, and standards. • Accuracy: Errors in tables, illustrations, or section references. • Usability: Suggestions to improve readability and navigation. Staff will continue reviewing formatting, numbering, hyperlinks, and other technical corrections. 3. Planning Commission Public Hearing and Recommendation Once the Planning Commission has completed its initial review and the draft is ready, a public hearing may be scheduled for the December meeting or a later meeting, with the required public notice. Following the public hearing, the Planning Commission may: 4. • Recommend the consolidated ordinance to the Township Board for readoption. • If additional revisions are needed, the Planning Commission may continue its review and postpone its recommendation to a subsequent meeting. Township Board Readoption Following the Planning Commission's recommendation and Township Attorney's review, the Township Board will consider repealing and readopting the consolidated Zoning Ordinance in its entirety, in accordance with applicable adoption procedures. Option 2: If additional time is needed to complete the review, the PC may set the public hearing at their December meeting. In that case, no action is required at this time. Page 9 of 26 SALINE TOWNSHIP WASHTENAW COUNTY, MICHIGAN NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING SALINE TOWNSHIP PLANNING COMMISSION Proposed Repeal and Readoption of the Consolidated Zoning Ordinance Date: ___; Time 7:00 p.m.; Location: Saline Township Hall, 5731 Braun Road, Saline, MI 48176 NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Saline Township Planning Commission will hold a public hearing to receive comments on the proposed repeal and readoption of the Saline Township Zoning Ordinance in its entirety. The proposed consolidated Zoning Ordinance incorporates previously adopted amendments into a single document and includes corrections to formatting, section numbering, cross-references, and other nonsubstantive errors. The purpose is to establish a complete, accurate, and accessible ordinance document. The ordinance does not proposes any changes to existing standards. The proposed ordinance applies throughout Saline Township. Following the public hearing, the Planning Commission may recommend the consolidated ordinance to the Township Board for readoption or postpone its recommendation pending further review. A copy of the proposed consolidated Zoning Ordinance is available for public review on the Township's website at https://salinetownship.org. Copies may also be reviewed by contacting the Township Clerk at 734-429-9968 to arrange an appointment. All interested persons are invited to attend the public hearing and provide comments. Written comments may be submitted to the Township Clerk at salinetownship@gmail.com before the public hearing. Individuals requiring assistance should contact the Township Clerk at 734-429-9968. Kelly Marion, Saline Township Clerk Stephen Rothfuss, Planning Commission Chair Publication Date: Posted Date: Page 10 of 26 Left blank on purpose Page 11 of 26 TO: Tom Hammond, Saline Township Supervisor FROM: Mike Auerbach, Planner DATE: October 22, 2026 RE: Zoning Ordinance Consolidation As requested by the Township, we have consolidated the Township’s zoning ordinance and available ordinance amendments into a single, comprehensive zoning ordinance document. The goal of this effort was to create a single ordinance document that reflects the current, effective Township Zoning Ordinance based on available Township records. Please note that reviewing the substantive content of the Ordinance was not a part of this project. The Ordinance document does not reflect our recommendations for best practices or regulatory changes that the Township should consider. PROCESS As a starting point, we used the Township’s Zoning Ordinance document that was published on the Township’s website, which indicates it was effective on February 1, 2008 and updated through September of 2017. The document was available as a downloadable zipped folder with the title “04-27-2018_9-5152_New Zoning Ordinance.” Next, we created a list of the subsequently adopted zoning ordinance amendments, which were also published on the Township’s website. We met with the Township Clerk to review the Township’s records of the adoption documents for each amendment. A list of those amendments is below. Please note that some of these amendments were subsequently repealed. Amendment Event Barn Amendment Energy Systems and Facilities Amendment to Section 11.10 Battery Energy Storage Systems Battery Energy Storage Systems Yard Encroachments Special Use Process Solar Energy Lot Splits Keeping of Animals Civil Infractions Home Occupations Sections 4.02, 5.113, 7.07, 18.02 4.02, 11.09, 11.10, 18.02 Ordinance 2026.01 2025.02 11.10 2024.02 4.02, 11.10, 12.01(B), 18.02 3.204 12.02 11.09 3.202 5.112 1.09(C)(2) 5.204, 18.02 2024.01 2023.01 2021.01 2017.03 2017.02 2017.01 2013.01 2011.03 Benjamin R. Carlisle, President John L. Enos, Vice President Douglas J. Lewan, Principal David Scurto, Principal Sally M. Elmiger, Principal R. Donald Wortman, Principal Craig Strong, Principal Paul Montagno, Principal Megan Masson-Minock, Principal Laura Kreps, Principal Richard K. Carlisle, Past President/Senior Principal Page 12 of 26 Zoning Ordinance Consolidation October 22, 2026 ORDINANCE DOCUMENT We have prepared two versions of the comprehensive ordinance document in Microsoft Word. The first identifies the edits we made to the “…New Zoning Ordinance” document using track changes, and includes comments with references to the applicable amendments or an explanation of the edit. The second version is a clean copy that reflects all of our edits. All of the changes have been accepted and the comments have been deleted. We also corrected non-substantive errors in the document such as misspellings, outdated section references, and inconsistencies in the section numbering hierarchy. Lastly, we incorporated section crossrefences which will function as hyperlinks. There are several non-substantive changes that we included in the document that we would like to bring to the Township’s attention: • • • • • We edited Section 1.06(B), Planning Commission Authority and Responsibilities to reflect the 2021.01 amendment granting the Township Board final approval authority over special land uses. The Use Table included references to solar energy systems that were not consistent with the 2025.02 Energy Systems and Facilities amendment. That text has been removed. We deleted Section 11.06, Wind Energy Conservation Systems, because those requirements are now redundant to the 2025.02 Energy Systems and Facilities requirements. Section 11.09 was repealed under 2025.02, and the new renewable energy provisions were adopted under Section 11.10. As a result, the Ordinance skipped Section 11.09. By deleting Section 11.06 as referenced above and renumbering the Article 11 sections in order, the Energy Systems and Facilities content is now Section 11.08. We have added the definition of event barns that the Planning Commission reviewed to Section 18.02. This change was referenced in the amendment public hearing notice and notice of adoption, but is not reflected in the 2026.01 ordinance document on the Township website. RECOMMENDATIONS Based on our review of the Township’s amendment records and the copy edits we identified in the Ordinance document, we recommend that the Township repeal and re-adopt the Ordinance in its entirety. While the Township has many of the records associated with each amendment, they are not complete. For example, the Township has records of the affidavits of publication that likely correspond to public hearing notices and notices of adoption, but copies of the notices themselves were not available in the Township’s records. While it may be possible to recover these records, readopting the Ordinance is a relatively quick and low-cost step to ensure it is properly adopted and in effect. Williamston, MI 48895 Subject: Data Center Regulations Dear Planning Commissioners: At the September meeting, the Planning Commission asked me to review two aspects of the proposed data center regulations: 1. Section 8.02(UU)(4)(c)(iv)(a), Maximum Sound Pressure Level. In the version reviewed by the Planning Commission in September, the maximum sound pressure level was set at 55 dBA during the day and 45 dBA at night. Trustee Creagh noted that these levels appeared to be inconsistent with the sound pressure levels recently established for other large-scale operations. I found that Trustee Creagh is correct: the maximum sound pressure level is 45 dBA during the day and at night for wind, solar, and energy storage systems. Therefore, to be consistent, we recommend changing the maximum sound pressure level for data centers to 45 dBA, day and night. 2. Section 8.02(UU)(4)(c)(iv)(c), Vibration. The regulations indicate that the Peak Particle Velocity (PPV) shall not exceed 0.01 inches per second. The Planning Commission questioned whether PPV is an appropriate measure of vibration and whether 0.01 inches per second is an appropriate standard. I have completed additional research on this, and found that a maximum PPV of 0.01 inches per second is probably the appropriate standard, but further discussion by the Planning Commission is required to determine if the PPV regulation should be retained. I found that PPV is most frequently used in the mining and construction industry to evaluate the potential damage ground vibration will cause to existing buildings. For example, PPV is often used to measure the impact of blasting in a mine on nearby structures. PPV is not the easiest subject to understand. If the Township adopts a PPV standard, an acoustical engineer will probably be required to enforce the regulations, as will become evident in the explanation below. PPV is a measurement of maximum ground particle movement speed. It is specified in the United States in inches per second, and in most of the rest of the world as millimeters per second. Measurements are made using a seismograph vibration meter. Here is where it gets complicated. PPV is a vector quantity (i.e., it has both a value and an associated direction). The three axes (directions) of measurement are the longitudinal, the transverse (the vector in the same plane as, but perpendicular to the longitudinal), and the vertical (up and down). All three are always measured and reported separately. An interesting fact is that not all vibrations felt by people are damaging to structures. Consequently, vibration standards attempt to separate those vibration intensities and frequencies that are potentially damaging to structures from those that are a concern to people. One source I found provided the following information about the effects of vibration on people at various PPV levels: Vibration Level (inches/sec) 0.0055 0.0118 0.0394 0.3937 Effect Vibration might be just perceptible in the most sensitive situations for most vibration frequencies associated with construction. Vibration might be just perceptible in residential environments. It is likely that vibration at this level in residential environments will cause complaints but can be tolerated if prior warning and explanation has been given to residents. Vibration is likely to be intolerable for any more than a very brief exposure. Please notice that the maximum PPV level set forth in the proposed regulations, 0.01 inches per second, is roughly comparable to “vibration might be just perceptible” in the chart above. One final feature of the PPV standard is worth noting: Ground vibration standards are properly used to judge the probability of a single ground vibration of a given size, duration, and frequency causing damage, rather than the probability of multiple or long-lasting vibrations causing damage. In summary, PPV is a complicated measuring tool that requires expert professional assistance to implement. On the other hand, it would provide an objective means of determining if a data center complies with vibration regulations. Use of PPV to measure the impact of vibration on people may be subject to challenge because this tool has not traditionally been used for this purpose. I look forward to reviewing this information with you on November 10th. Sincerely, McKENNA Christopher J. Revisions to Article 24.00, GD, Green Zone ... 16 Williamstown Township, Ingham County, MI Data Center Regulations August 31, 2026 WILLIAMSTOWN TOWNSHIP ZONING ORDINANCE Data Center Regulations INTRODUCTION This document contains recommended zoning regulations for various types of data centers. The regulations would be inserted in Article 8.00 of the Zoning Ordinance, which deals with Site Development Standards Applicable to Specific Uses. We propose to create a new subsection UU within Section 8.02. UU. Data Centers 1. Purpose. The purpose of this subsection is to establish regulations for the design, placement, and operation of data centers in Williamstown Township. Data centers have high energy and water needs, can generate noise that may be heard off-site, have high security needs, and have special building features that create land use impacts that must be managed. The regulations in this subsection are intended to: a. Ensure compatibility with surrounding land uses. b. Manage land use impacts, including but not limited to noise, water usage, hazardous materials use, lighting, and energy usage. c. Protect public health, safety, and welfare. 2. Definitions. The following words and terms, when used in this subsection, shall have the meanings ascribed to them, except where the context clearly indicates a different meaning: Community Benefits Agreement: A legally binding contract between a data center developer or owner and the Township, in which the Township seeks benefits in exchange for good faith cooperation in project approval and permitting. Benefits may include, but are not limited to, workforce commitments, funding for affordable housing, and infrastructure improvements (such as road improvements), and natural resource enhancements. Cooling System: Any system, equipment, or apparatus used to regulate temperature or humidity within a data center, including but not limited to air conditioning, cooling towers, and liquid cooling systems. Data Center: A facility designed for storage, processing, and transmission of digital data. A data center typically houses servers, hard drives, networking equipment, and other components related to digital data operations. Data center Williamstown Township, Ingham County, MI Data Center Regulations October 15, 2026 Page 1 infrastructure may also include air handling equipment, power generators, water cooling and storage facilities, utility substations, and other related support equipment. For the purposes of this subsection, the following types of data centers have been identified: a. Enterprise Data Center (also known as an On-Premise Data Center). An enterprise data center is a private data center facility that supports a single business or organization. Enterprise data centers are custom built to be compatible with the business or organization’s distinctive enterprise apps and processes. Enterprise data centers typically occupy less than 5,000 sq. ft. of space and typically operate on less than 100-150 kW of power. b. Multi-Tenant or Colocation Data Center. A multi-tenant or colocation data center offers data center space to businesses that want to host their computing hardware and servers offsite. These facilities provide the proper components—power, cooling, securing, and networking components— needed to do so. Companies that don’t have the space for their own enterprise data center, or an IT team dedicated to manage it, often choose a multi-tenant or colocation data center. A multi-tenant or colocation data center typically operates on 10 to 60 MW of power. c. Hyperscale Data Center. A hyperscale data center is one that typically occupies one or more warehouse-sized buildings, and houses thousands of servers to handle very large processing workloads. A hyperscale data center typically operates on 100 MW of power or greater. d. Edge or Micro Data Center. Edge data centers are small data centers built near the people or business they are intended to serve, providing real-time data processing, analysis, and action, making low-latency communication with smart devices possible. Edge data centers typically operate on less than 100-150 kW of power. e. Container or Modular Data Center.
